The airplane impacted a grass field on a heading of 056° magnetic, parallel to a tree line with the landing gear retracted. The initial ground scar consisted of a propeller strike, and one propeller blade was separated. The right wing struck the base of a tree and the right auxiliary fuel tank was breached. The engine sustained impact damage from a tree at the No. 2 cylinder, which was separated from its mounts. The airplane’s left horizontal stabilizer also contained damage consistent with a tree strike and it came to rest against a tree at the edge of a dry creek bed. The airplane was destroyed by a postimpact fire. The wreckage was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260629203271.s: Two pilots were fatally injured when their Bellanca 14-19-2, N9846B, crashed shortly after takeoff from Goldsby, Oklahoma, during a personal flight. The aircraft climbed slowly, turned left, then descended rapidly into trees, sustaining impact damage and a post-crash fire.

NTSB:20260630203282.n: On June 25, 2026, about 1125 mountain standard time, a Beech S35, N6040F, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Dome, Arizona. The pilot and three passengers were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported that he departed Eagle Roost Airport (27AZ), Aguila, Arizona, for a cross-country flight to Yuma Marine Corps Air Station/Yuma International Airport (YNK), Yuma, Arizona. According to the pilot, about 15 nm northeast of YNK the engine began to run rough, so he enriched the mixture to smooth out the engine. The pilot then decided to perform a precautionary landing and landed the airplane on a dirt road with the landing gear retracted. Shortly after touchdown, the airplane veered right off the road and came to rest upright in a ditch. Subsequently, the right wing was substantially damaged. The airplane was recovered to a secure facility for further examination.
NTSB:20260630203282.s: The pilot of a Beech S35 operating a Part 91 flight reported engine roughness near Yuma, Arizona, and executed a precautionary landing on a dirt road with gear retracted. The aircraft veered off the road into a ditch, sustaining substantial damage to the right wing, though all four occupants were uninjured.

NTSB:20260630203283.n: On June 29, 2026, about 1148 Pacific daylight Time, a MTO Sport gyroplane, N423AG, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident at Reid-Hillview Airport (RHV), San Jose, California. The pilot was seriously injured, and the passenger received minor injuries. The gyroplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the pilot, the purpose of the flight was to take a passenger on a local traffic pattern flight to demonstrate the gyroplane. The pilot reported that the pre-flight inspection, engine start, run-up, magneto check, and pre-takeoff checks revealed no anomalies. Before taking off from runway 14L, he engaged the secondary fuel pump. The pilot stated that the takeoff roll was normal; however, when the main landing gear was about 6 inches above the runway, the radio lost power. He attempted to reset the radio power but was unable to restore it, which he believed was indicative of a master power failure. As the gyroplane approached the departure end of the runway about 130 ft above ground level, the pilot noticed that the gyroplane was no longer climbing and had entered a slight descent. He selected a dirt area off the runway for a forced landing. The gyroplane continued to descend and impacted terrain at about 15 mph. Resulting in substantial damage to the fuselage and main rotor system. The wreckage was recovered to a secure location for further examination.
NTSB:20260630203283.s: During a local traffic pattern flight in a MTO Sport gyroplane, the pilot experienced a master power failure shortly after takeoff from runway 14L at Reid-Hillview Airport. The aircraft entered a descent and impacted terrain during a forced landing, causing substantial damage and injuring the pilot and passenger.

NTSB:20260630203284.n: On June 30, 2026, at about 1030 eastern daylight time, an experimental Sonerai 2 airplane, N1406, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Cynthiana, Kentucky. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported that the purpose of the flight was to perform local air work in the traffic pattern. There were no anomalies noted during the preflight inspection, engine run-up, or subsequent takeoff. The airplane departed with 10 gallons of fuel. About 25 minutes into the flight, after completing two touch-and-go-landings, the airplane experienced a total loss of engine power while transitioning to the crosswind leg of the traffic pattern. The pilot was unable to restore engine power and performed a forced landing to a field west of the airport. During the landing roll, the landing gear separated and the fuselage impacted the ground resulting in substantial damage to the fuselage. Following the landing, the airplane's lithium battery caught fire and consumed most of the fuselage. The wreckage was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260630203284.s: The pilot of an experimental Sonerai 2, N1406, suffered a total engine power loss during a local air work flight near Cynthiana, Kentucky. The subsequent forced landing caused landing gear separation and fuselage damage, followed by a lithium battery fire that consumed most of the aircraft.

NTSB:20260630203285.n: The pilot of the tailwheel-equipped airplane reported that, during the landing roll, a strong gust of wind lifted the right wing, which resulted in the left wing tip striking the ground adjacent to the runway. The pilot initiated a go-around; however, after the airplane became airborne, the wind pushed the airplane to the left, and it settled into a ditch on the left side of the runway. Upon exiting the ditch, the airplane became airborne, and the wind pushed the airplane toward an airport perimeter fence. Subsequently, the left main landing gear struck the fence and the airplane nosed over which resulted in substantial damage to both wings, left horizontal stabilizer, and left elevator. At the time of the accident, the pilot was landing the airplane on runway 17 with wind from 250° at 9 knots, gusting to 18 knots. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260630203285.s: The pilot of a tailwheel airplane experienced a left wingtip strike and subsequent ditching during landing on Runway 17 due to strong gusts. The aircraft later struck a perimeter fence and nosed over, causing substantial damage to the wings and tail, with no mechanical malfunctions reported.

NTSB:20260630203286.n: The pilot of the tailwheel equipped airplane performed a three-point landing and flared a little high which led to a few mild bounces. Shortly after, the airplane veered left and the pilot applied corrective control inputs. Subsequently, the airplane veered hard right, exited the runway, and ground looped. During the ground loop, the left wing impacted the ground which resulted in substantial damage to the left wing and fuselage. The pilot reported no pre-accident mechanical failures or malfunctions that would have precluded normal operation. At the time of the accident, the pilot was landing on runway 17 with wind from 250° at 8 knots.
NTSB:20260630203286.s: The pilot of a tailwheel airplane ground looped and exited runway 17 after veering hard right following a high flare and mild bounces. The left wing impacted the ground, causing substantial damage to the wing and fuselage, with no pre-accident mechanical failures reported.

NTSB:20260630203288.n: The pilot reported that, after flying most of the cross-country flight with the fuel selector set to the right fuel tank, he entered an extended downwind for landing at the destination airport. Just before turning base, the right fuel tank became empty and the engine stopped. He immediately turned the fuel selector to the left tank and attempted to restart the engine but was unsuccessful. He reported hearing the stall warning horn before the airplane "dropped out from under" him and impacted a dry riverbed, resulting in substantial damage to the fuselage and wings. The pilot reported that his improper fuel management resulted in fuel starvation and the subsequent loss of engine power. He further remarked that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260630203288.s: The pilot experienced an engine stoppage during an extended downwind due to fuel starvation after the right tank emptied. He failed to restart the engine, resulting in a stall and impact with a dry riverbed that caused substantial damage to the fuselage and wings.

NTSB:20260630203291.n: The pilot of the tailwheel equipped airplane reported that after they performed a 3-point landing, the airplane veered to the right. The pilot attempted to correct with left rudder input; however, the airplane continued to the right and exited the runway surface. The left main landing gear dug into the grass covered surface and the airplane pivoted 180° to the right, which resulted in substantial damage to the left aileron and left elevator. Post accident examination revealed that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunction or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. At the time of the accident, the pilot was landing on runway 27, with wind variable at 5 knots.
NTSB:20260630203291.s: The pilot of a tailwheel airplane veered right after a 3-point landing on runway 27, exiting the surface despite left rudder input. The aircraft pivoted 180° in grass, damaging the left aileron and elevator, with no pre-accident mechanical failures found.

NTSB:20260630203293.n: On June 29, 2026, about 1945 eastern daylight time (EDT), a Diamond Aircraft Industries Inc. DA40 NG airplane, N602RF, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Petersburg, Virginia. The flight instructor sustained serious injuries, and the student pilot sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight. The flight instructor reported that during the initial climb following a go-around on Runway 05 at Dinwiddie County Airport (PTB), the occupants heard a loud bang near midfield, followed by a reduction in engine power. The flight instructor assumed control of the airplane and observed that engine power decreased to below about 40%, resulting in a loss of expected climb performance; the engine continued to produce partial power. The airplane was unable to achieve sufficient climb performance to clear obstacles beyond the departure end of the runway environment. While assessing available areas for a forced landing, the flight instructor maneuvered the airplane, which resulted in activation of the stall warning horn. The flight instructor discontinued the turn and secured the engine by moving the fuel selector to the off position before the airplane impacted treetops. The airplane came to rest inverted in a densely wooded area about 1 mile northeast of the departure end of Runway 05, which resulted in substantial damage to the fuselage, wings, and empennage. A data card from the avionics installed in the airplane was retained and forwarded to the NTSB Recorders Laboratory for flight and engine data extraction. The wreckage has been recovered to a secure facility for further examination.
NTSB:20260630203293.s: During a Part 91 instructional flight in a Diamond DA40 NG, a flight instructor and student pilot sustained injuries after a loud bang caused engine power to drop below 40% during climb following a go-around. The instructor attempted a forced landing but the aircraft stalled, impacted treetops, and came to rest inverted with substantial damage.

NTSB:20260701203294.n: The flight instructor and the student pilot had just completed a training flight, but still needed to fly back to their home airport. A friend of the pilot sat in the back of the airplane during the training flight. The student pilot asked the instructor if his friend, who had no flight training experience other than a discovery flight, could sit up front for the return flight. The instructor agreed and provided clear instructions to the friend to not touch any of the flight controls during the flight. The friend was asked if he had any questions about the takeoff and he said he had none. During the takeoff roll, the instructor said the friend tapped the left brake with his foot, which resulted in a "slight bump" of the airplane. This motion scared the friend, who then panicked and grabbed the control yoke and pulled it all the way back while moving it to the left. The left wing briefly touched the ground and the friend repeatedly screamed, "I' m sorry!" The friend did not let go of the controls, and the instructor had to wrestle him and repeatedly tell him to let go and that he had the controls. The instructor said he needed both hands to try and overcome the force the friend had on the controls. The instructor was able to get the airplane's wings level just before it collided with a fence, which resulted in substantial damage to the wings and fuselage. The friend told first responders that he was the one that crashed the airplane and that "it was all his fault.
NTSB:20260701203294.s: During takeoff, a passenger in the front seat of a training aircraft grabbed the controls and pulled back after accidentally tapping the brake, causing the left wing to strike the ground. The flight instructor wrestled for control but the aircraft subsequently collided with a fence, resulting in substantial damage to the wings and fuselage.

NTSB:20260701203300.n: The pilot reported that during the initial approach, he was given vectors from air traffic control (ATC) that took him about 15 miles away from the airport. As he was vectored back toward the airport, ATC notified him that he was fifth in sequence to land and was asked to decrease airspeed. About 5 miles from the airport, ATC turned multiple airplanes in front of him, and he continued to maintain visual contact with each airplane. The spacing was tight with airplane in front of him and he continued to watch it as it slowly exited the runway. While on short final, he forgot to complete the before landing checklist, which resulted in him not extending the landing gear. The airplane landed on its belly and came to rest upright on the runway, which resulted in substantial damage to the bottom fuselage. The pilot reported no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260701203300.s: During the initial approach, the pilot was vectored by ATC and faced tight spacing before forgetting to complete the before landing checklist on short final. This omission resulted in landing gear not being extended, causing the aircraft to land on its belly and sustain substantial fuselage damage.

NTSB:20260701203301.n: On June 30, 2026, about 1745 central daylight time, a Beech A36, N8095F, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident at Paynesville Municipal Airport (PEX), Paynesville, Minnesota. The private pilot and one passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported that after landing on runway 29, the airplane began to oscillate vertically during the landing roll. The nose landing gear subsequently collapsed, and the airplane skidded to a stop on the runway. The pilot and passenger exited the airplane without injury. Examination by a Federal Aviation Administration inspector revealed that the nose landing gear had fractured and separated from the airplane. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the forward fuselage. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260701203301.s: A private pilot flying a Beech A36 experienced vertical oscillation during the landing roll on runway 29 at Paynesville Municipal Airport, causing the nose landing gear to fracture and collapse. The aircraft skidded to a stop with substantial forward fuselage damage, but the pilot and passenger exited without injury.

NTSB:20260702203306.n: On July 2, 2026, at 0052 eastern daylight time (EDT), a Beech model 95-A55 airplane, N7501S, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Lancaster, South Carolina. Both pilots received serious injuries. The accident flight was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 91 personal flight. The airplane owner reported that the pilots were renting the airplane for the purpose of building multiengine flight experience. Preliminary ADS-B data indicated that three flights prior to the accident flight were conducted on July 1, 2026. The first flight departed from the Stanly County Airport (VUJ), Albemarle, North Carolina, at 0707 EDT on July 1, 2026, arriving at the Copiah County Airport (M11), Crystal Springs, Mississippi, at 0939 central daylight time (CDT). The second flight departed M11 at 1008 CDT, arriving at Laredo International Airport (LRD), Laredo, Texas, landing at 1336 CDT. The third flight departed LRD at 1553 CDT and arrived at the Poplarville/Pearl River County Airport (M13), Poplarville, Mississippi, landing at 1941 CDT. The airport manager at M13 confirmed that 106 gallons of 100LL aviation fuel was added to the airplane while it was on the ground at M13. At 2017 CDT, the airplane departed M13 on the accident flight with VUJ as the intended destination. ADS-B data showed that the airplane proceeded east-northeast until 0043 EDT on July 2, 2026, when it made a left turn to a heading of about 025°. Shortly, thereafter, the airplane turned further left to a westerly heading. At 0046, the crew declared an emergency and advised air traffic control (ATC) services that they were going to divert to Kirk Air Base Airport (T73), Lancaster, South Carolina, due to issues with both engines. When the airplane was about 2 nm north of T73, they advised that they would instead divert to the Lancaster County Airport-Mc Whirter Field (LKR), Lancaster, South Carolina. ADS-B data showed that the airplane continued descending and the final recorded location was about 4 nm and 105° from LKR. The accident location was 0.2 nm west of the final recorded ADS-B position (see figure 1). Figure 1. Google Earth plot of the final portion of the accident flight. The airplane came to rest on a wooded hillside. There was evidence of a postimpact fire that consumed most of the cabin section of the airplane. The forward part of the airplane’s fuselage, including the baggage compartment, cabin and nose were almost completely consumed by the postimpact fire. The aft fuselage was predominately intact. The left horizontal stabilizer and elevator, along with the vertical stabilizer and rudder, remained attached to the aft fuselage. The right horizontal stabilizer and elevator had separated from the airplane and was located in the immediate area of the main wreckage. The left wing remained partially attached by control cables; however, the inboard portion of the wing between the engine nacelle and the fuselage side was mostly consumed by fire but was otherwise intact to the left-wing tip. The left engine nacelle from the firewall aft was attached to the wing but the engine had separated. The landing gear was present at the accident site but its position could not be determined during the on-scene phase of the examination. The cockpit and cabin section of the fuselage was almost completely consumed by the postimpact fire. Both engines were present near the main wreckage. The outboard portion of the right wing from about the flap/aileron joint was separated and located in the immediate area of the main wreckage. The inboard portion of the right wing, including the engine nacelle aft of the firewall was mostly consumed by the postimpact fire. The engine and firewall came to rest near the main wreckage. A portion of the right-wing flap came to rest near the separated portion of the right wing. On-scene examination was limited due to the location of the wreckage and the prevailing terrain. The wreckage was recovered for further examination. First responders reported that the pilots were outside of the airplane before they arrived and there was no information as to which seats the pilots occupied. Therefore, it is unknown which pilot was manipulating the flight controls at the time of the accident. Both pilots received severe burns and were transported to a hospital burn unit for treatment. One pilot held a commercial pilot certificate with airplane single engine land, multiengine land, and instrument airplane ratings. He also had a second-class medical certificate issued March 2026. The other pilot held a commercial pilot certificate with airplane single engine land, multiengine land, and instrument airplane ratings. He also held a flight instructor certificate with airplane single engine and instrument ratings. The airplane owner reported that this pilot had recently received his flight instructor rating for multiengine land airplanes. He also had a first-class medical certificate issued February 2026.
NTSB:20260702203306.s: Two commercial pilots flying a rented Beech 95-A55 experienced dual engine failure during a night cross-country flight, forcing an emergency diversion. The aircraft crashed into a wooded hillside near Lancaster, South Carolina, resulting in serious burns to both pilots and a postimpact fire that destroyed the airplane.

NTSB:20260702203308.n: On July 2, 2026, at 1032 central daylight time, a Cirrus Design Corp SR22, N127DC, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Lafayette, Tennessee. The pilot and passenger sustained no injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulation Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported that following the completion of an annual inspection, he was returning a ferry pilot to Owensboro/Davis County Regional Airport (OWB), Owensboro, Kentucky. About 20 minutes into the flight, while at an altitude of 6,500 feet mean sea level, the engine completely lost power. The pilot initially attempted to divert to the nearest airport, which was about 12 miles away, but then determined they would be unable to reach the airport. The pilot then made a distress call to air traffic control and decided to activate the airplane's whole airframe parachute system at an altitude of 1,975 feet. The parachute successfully deployed and the airplane came to rest in a tree within an urban neighborhood. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the empennage, fuselage, and wings. The airplane was recovered and retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260702203308.s: A pilot ferrying a Cirrus SR22 experienced a complete engine power loss at 6,500 feet MSL. The pilot deployed the whole airframe parachute at 1,975 feet, resulting in a substantial damage crash into a tree with no injuries to the occupants.

NTSB:20260705203311.n: On July 4, 2026, about 0942 central daylight time, a Piper PA-25-235 airplane, N386AB, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Forest Lake, Minnesota. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations part 91 banner tow flight. The pilot reported that he completed a normal preflight inspection and engine runup. After a successful banner hook, the airplane struggled to climb. The pilot increased the throttle and fuel mixture to full, but the airplane could not maintain level flight. The pilot jettisoned the banner, and the airplane continued to lose altitude. The pilot conducted a forced landing into trees resulting in substantial damage to both wings, rudder, and vertical stabilizer. Postaccident examination of the engine and airframe revealed no mechanical anomalies that would have precluded normal operation. According to FAA Special Airworthiness Bulletin CE-09-35, weather at the time of the accident was conducive to the formation of serious icing at glide power. The pilot reported that he did not turn on the carburetor heat when troubleshooting the loss of engine power.
NTSB:20260705203311.s: The pilot of a Piper PA-25-235 conducting a banner tow flight experienced power loss and could not maintain level flight due to suspected icing. After jettisoning the banner, the pilot forced-landed into trees, causing substantial damage, as post-accident inspection found no mechanical anomalies.

NTSB:20260705203312.n: According to the flight instructor, the student pilot aligned the weight-shift control trike with the runway centerline and began the takeoff roll. As the speed increased, the student pilot began moving the control bar forward to the liftoff position. It was then that something did not seem right. The flight instructor directed the student pilot to reduce engine power and reject the takeoff. It was then that the aircraft made a "snap" turn to the right and rolled onto its left side damaging the left wing. The flight instructor stated there were no mechanical failures or malfunctions with respect to the aircraft before the accident. He noted that the student pilot may have inadvertently had pressure against the left pedal which caused the snap turn to the right when he reduced throttle, which was on the left. The flight instructor stated further that if the student pilot had been instructed to reduce engine power slowly while maintaining the runway centerline, the accident might have been prevented. The aircraft flight manual noted that, with respect to ground handling, left pedal pressure corresponded to right taxi steering. Similarly, right pedal pressure corresponded to left taxi steering.
NTSB:20260705203312.s: A student pilot and flight instructor rejected a weight-shift trike takeoff due to an abnormal feel, causing the aircraft to snap right and roll onto its left wing. The instructor attributed the accident to inadvertent left pedal pressure by the student, which steered the aircraft right upon throttle reduction.

NTSB:20260706203314.n: On July 4, 2026, about 1121 eastern daylight time, an experimental amateur-built Flight Star II SC airplane, N432JP, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Mulberry, Florida. The private pilot and a passenger were seriously injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot stated that he fueled the airplane, performed a preflight inspection, and completed a safety briefing with the passenger. He started the engine and taxied to the runway where he completed an engine runup and a flight control systems check, noting that all instrument indications were normal. He communicated his intentions to take off on runway 14 and began his takeoff roll. The pilot rotated the airplane at 60 mph and established a positive rate of climb. Suddenly, the airplane started to descend. He described the feeling like being on an elevator. The pilot stated that he had felt this before at a neighboring airport during landing. Powerlines obstructed the direction of flight, and unable to climb above the obstruction, the pilot turned the airplane to the right attempting to fly between the poles. The right wing contacted a wire, before the airplane descended and impacted the ground. The airplane came to rest on a roadway on its side and incurred substantial damage to both wings and the fuselage. A witness, who was also a pilot, observed the takeoff. He stated that the airplane appeared to maintain a reduced rate of climb relative to its observed pitch attitude. As the airplane passed abeam his position, it began to descend. Throughout the observed sequence, he did not perceive any changes in engine sound. The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260706203314.s: A private pilot and passenger were seriously injured when their experimental Flight Star II SC descended shortly after takeoff near Mulberry, Florida. The pilot attributed the loss of climb to an unexplained elevator-like sensation, leading to a right-wing strike on powerlines and a subsequent ground impact.

NTSB:20260706203316.n: At the conclusion of a local flight the pilot was returning to his private grass airstrip. He reported the wind was gusting to about 13 knots, and while on short final approach to land, he felt that the wind died abruptly and the airplane "lost lift." The airplane descended before contacting a field of soybeans just short of the runway. The airplane then nosed over and came to rest near the approach end of the runway. The pilot was seriously injured and airplane sustained substantial damage to the vertical empennage, rudder, and wing struts. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260706203316.s: During a local flight, a pilot landing a private aircraft on a grass strip encountered an abrupt wind die-out on short final, causing a loss of lift. The airplane struck soybeans, nosed over, and sustained substantial damage, resulting in serious injury to the pilot with no reported mechanical failures.

NTSB:20260706203317.n: The pilot reported that upon touching down on the turf runway, the tailwheel-equipped airplane began a "moderate excursion to the right" and that he applied left rudder and brakes to correct. The airplane then veered left and nosed over resulting in substantial damage to the left wing and the lift struts of both wings. The pilot stated that the turf along the airplane's landing roll path was "torn up," and was likely the result of excessive braking. The pilot also reported that while he had extensive experience flying tailwheel equipped airplanes they had all been fitted with modern hydraulically actuated braking systems, while the accident airplane was equipped with the original mechanical/drum brakes. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260706203317.s: The pilot of a tailwheel-equipped airplane nosed over on a turf runway after excessive braking caused the aircraft to veer left following an initial right excursion. The pilot attributed the loss of control to unfamiliarity with the aircraft's original mechanical drum brakes compared to modern hydraulic systems, resulting in substantial wing damage.

NTSB:20260706203318.n: The flight instructor and pilot receiving instruction were conducting touch-and-go takeoffs and landings in the airport traffic pattern to familiarize the pilot with a recently purchased airplane. The flight instructor reported that, on the final landing, the pilot pitched the nose of the airplane up too aggressively for the flare. As a result of the high nose up attitude the airplane stalled, landed hard, and bounced back into the air. The pilot applied full engine power; however, the airplane remained in a nose up attitude, yawed to right, and bounced a second time. Subsequently, the airplane exited the runway surface and the right wing collided with an airport sign, which resulted in substantial damage to the right wing. According to the flight instructor, after the second bounced landing, he directed the pilot to reduce the throttle to idle. The flight instructor added that on his side of the airplane he did not have access to the throttle or brakes, only shared access to the center control stick. The pilot receiving instruction reported that there were no mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260706203318.s: A flight instructor and student pilot conducting touch-and-go landings in a new airplane experienced a hard landing and runway excursion after the student flared too aggressively, causing a stall and bounce. The aircraft subsequently struck an airport sign with the right wing, resulting in substantial damage.

NTSB:20260706203319.n: The pilot reported that during landing rollout the airplane veered left upon touchdown. Despite the pilot's application of right rudder, the deviation continued and progressed into a ground loop after the tailwheel contacted the runway. The airplane subsequently departed the runway, and the left wing and elevator impacted terrain, resulting in substantial damage to the left wing. The pilot reported no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260706203319.s: The pilot reported that during landing rollout, the aircraft veered left despite right rudder application, ground-looped after tailwheel contact, and departed the runway. The left wing and elevator struck terrain causing substantial damage, with no pre-accident mechanical failures reported.

NTSB:20260706203320.n: The pilot of the amphibious airplane reported that he performed a go-around during the first approach to the river seaplane base as the water did not look good (choppy). The water looked good during the second approach and the airplane touched down smooth, but the pilot did not see a large wave off the left side due to flat light, and the left float contacted the wave. The contact resulted in the airplane bouncing up into the air and contacting the water a second time, resulting in a hard landing and collapsed left float strut. The hard landing also resulted in substantial damage to the left elevator. The pilot added that there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260706203320.s: The pilot of an amphibious airplane executed a go-around on the first approach due to choppy water but struck a large wave on the second approach due to flat light. This caused a hard landing that collapsed the left float strut and damaged the left elevator, with no preimpact mechanical malfunctions reported.

NTSB:20260706203322.n: The purpose of the flight was for the pilot to familiarize himself with the experimental air racing airplane after the airplane had been in storage, and the pilot had not flown the airplane in over two years. The airplane was assembled by the air racing team, all the flight controls were checked, and the engine was run up. The pilot insisted on flying the airplane, even though the airplane maintenance records were not completed. The pilot had intended on staying in the airport traffic pattern. During the initial climb, witnesses reported the airplane's critical angle of attack was exceeded, and the airplane entered an aerodynamic stall at a low altitude. The airplane impacted a flat field with vegetation, on airport property. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage and to both wings. The pilot, who was wearing an airplane flight helmet, was unable to recall all the accident sequence details due to sustained serious injuries. The pilot reported there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airframe or the engine that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260706203322.s: The pilot of an experimental air racing airplane stalled during initial climb after exceeding the critical angle of attack while attempting a familiarization flight. The aircraft impacted a field on airport property, sustaining substantial damage, with the pilot reporting no preimpact mechanical failures.

NTSB:20260706203329.n: On July 5, 2026, at about 0825 Pacific daylight time, a Piper PA-28-140, N3995K, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Salome, Arizona. The pilot and passenger were uninjured. The airplane was operating as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the passenger, who was a rated pilot and mechanic, the purpose of the flight was to conduct an engine break-in flight following a recent engine overhaul. Before the flight, the pilot and passenger completed a preflight inspection and engine ground run, during which no anomalies were noted. The magneto checks were within specifications, with an approximate 100-rpm drop, and the passenger did not observe any abnormal engine temperature or oil pressure indications. The passenger reported that he had previously conducted ground runs on the engine following the overhaul, and they were normal. The airplane departed from runway 17 at Western Sky Airpark (OAZ2), Salome, Arizona. The passenger described the takeoff as normal and stated that the engine was producing about 2,400 rpm, with the throttle full forward and the mixture full rich. At about 800 to 900 ft above ground level, the pilot turned the airplane to the right and began reducing the throttle from full power. The passenger estimated the throttle reduction at about 200 rpm, though he did not recall the exact rpm amount. Immediately after the throttle was reduced, the engine lost all power. The passenger reported there were no indications of an impending engine failure, including no unusual vibration, smoke, sounds, or abnormal gauge readings. The pilot then searched for a forced landing area. The passenger estimated that about 20 to 30 seconds later the airplane impacted terrain. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the wings, fuselage, tail, and empennage. The wreckage was recovered to a secure location for further examination.
NTSB:20260706203329.s: A Piper PA-28-140 pilot and passenger experienced total engine power loss at 800–900 feet AGL shortly after reducing throttle during a post-overhaul break-in flight. The aircraft subsequently impacted terrain near Salome, Arizona, sustaining substantial damage, though both occupants remained uninjured.

NTSB:20260707203331.n: As the pilot approached the 1,997 ft-long, turf runway at the destination airport, and was turning from the base leg of the traffic pattern to the final approach, he heard another pilot report over the airport's common traffic advisory frequency that they were on final approach to an intersecting runway. He immediately reduced his descent while he communicated with the other pilot before resuming the landing attempt. The resulting final approach was steeper than normal and the pilot touched down with insufficient remaining runway, which resulted in the airplane overrunning the runway and impacting trees. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the engine mount, left wing, and fuselage. The pilot reported that there were no mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260707203331.s: The pilot, while turning base to final on a 1,997 ft turf runway, heard another aircraft on an intersecting final approach. After reducing descent to communicate, the pilot executed a steep approach, overran the runway, and impacted trees, causing substantial damage to the engine mount, left wing, and fuselage.

NTSB:20260707203336.n: The student pilot reported that he extended the downwind leg to accommodate a departing tow airplane. During the subsequent approach, the glider was high. The pilot did not use the dive brakes to reduce altitude and attempted a forward slip; however, the glider remained high and fast throughout the approach. As a result, the glider touched down near the end and right side of the runway. During the subsequent landing rollout, the right wing struck a person on the ground, which resulted in serious injury. The glider then ground looped and sustained substantial damage to the right wing. The pilot reported no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the glider that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260707203336.s: A student pilot flying a glider extended the downwind leg for a departing tow plane, resulting in a high, fast approach without dive brake use. The glider landed near the runway end, struck a person on the ground causing serious injury, and ground looped with substantial wing damage.

NTSB:20260707203339.n: The pilot reported that before departing for a local flight, he repositioned the helicopter to the fuel station. While preparing to refuel, the pilot discovered the fueling hose was too short to reach the helicopter. The pilot instructed the passenger to exit the helicopter so he could reposition it closer to the fuel pump. After lifting into a low hover, the helicopter turned, and the main rotor blades struck a tree. The helicopter then impacted a second tree. The pilot maneuvered the helicopter away from the fuel station, landed hard, and the helicopter rolled onto its side. The helicopter sustained substantial damage to the tailboom and main rotor blades. The pilot reported that there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures with the helicopter that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260707203339.s: During a local flight preparation, a helicopter pilot repositioned the aircraft to refuel but struck two trees with the main rotor blades while hovering. The helicopter subsequently landed hard, rolled onto its side, and sustained substantial damage to the tailboom and rotor blades with no reported mechanical failures.

NTSB:20260707203340.n: The pilot of the tailwheel-equipped airplane reported that, during the landing roll, the left wing was lifted by a wind gust, and the airplane began to veer to the left. Despite the pilot's left flaperon input and application of right rudder, the airplane ground looped to the left. Subsequently, the right wing contacted the runway and the landing gear collapsed, resulting in substantial damage to the right wing and fuselage. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical failures or malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. At the time of the accident, the pilot was landing the airplane on runway 05, with the winds from 330° at 3 knots gusting 14 Knots.
NTSB:20260707203340.s: The pilot of a tailwheel airplane ground looped left during landing on runway 05 due to a wind gust lifting the left wing. Despite control inputs, the right wing contacted the runway, collapsing the gear and causing substantial damage with no mechanical failures reported.

NTSB:20260707203342.n: On July 7, 2026, about 1259 mountain daylight time, an Air Tractor, Inc. AT-502B airplane, N647LA, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Ogden, Utah. The commercial pilot was not injured. The flight was conducted as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 137 aerial application flight. The pilot reported that before takeoff, the left brake felt less effective than normal. He performed a brake check and subsequently departed to conduct a mosquito spray operation. During the takeoff roll, the pilot felt an abnormal flutter in the left brake pedal and considered aborting the takeoff. However, given the airplane’s weight, speed and position on the runway, he determined that continuing the takeoff presented less risk than attempting to stop. After departure, he sent a text message to company maintenance personnel advising that he suspected a problem with the left brake and that it would require inspection. Upon returning to the airport he performed a wheel landing, during which the main landing gear contacted the runway before the tailwheel. After the tailwheel settled onto the runway, the airplane began veering to the right. The pilot applied full left rudder, followed by left brake; however, the airplane continued to veer right. He then applied reverse engine thrust to further slow the airplane’s speed. The left main landing gear subsequently collapsed, and the airplane rotated about 180° to the right, which resulted in substantial damage to the fuselage, left wing, and left aileron. The airplane then exited the runway and came to rest near the right side runway edge. Postaccident examination of the left main gear assembly revealed that the wheel hub grease cap, cotter pin, wheel nut and outer wheel bearing were missing from the left wheel axle assembly. The outer face of the wheel exhibited impact gouges, and the brake components had a dark, wet appearance. The backing plate attached to the main landing gear spring exhibited a crack that ran the length of the plate. A search of the airport grounds did not locate the missing components. The left main landing gear assembly was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260707203342.s: A commercial pilot flying an Air Tractor AT-502B on an aerial application mission experienced left brake failure and gear collapse during landing rollout. The accident, causing substantial damage, resulted from missing wheel hub components and a cracked backing plate that prevented directional control.

NTSB:20260708203349.n: The pilot/operator commanded the takeoff sequence on the agricultural unmanned aircraft system (UAS) and the UAS climbed to about 15 ft above its launch rig. Hearing an abnormal "popping" noise coming from the UAS, the pilot initiated the automated landing sequence and the UAS descended to about 2 ft above the rig and about 4 to 5 ft from the operator's station. The pilot lost control of the UAS as it moved towards his position causing the pilot to duck behind the operator's barrier. When he ducked, the UAS's right-rear propeller struck his left hand resulting in a serious injury. The UAS descended and crashed into terrain resulting in substantial damage to the right-rear arm and propeller. The operator sent the UAS on-board data to the manufacturer for decoding. The manufacturer's report found that about 1 second after the UAS started up, a joystick input was received which paused the UAS's takeoff. A couple seconds later, additional control inputs were recorded and the UAS responded accordingly. The data found no mechanical malfunction or failure with all engine parameters in the normal range.
NTSB:20260708203349.s: The pilot operating an agricultural UAS lost control during takeoff after hearing a popping noise, causing the aircraft to strike his hand and crash. Manufacturer data analysis revealed no mechanical failure, attributing the incident to recorded joystick inputs that paused and altered the flight path.

NTSB:20260708203350.n: The flight instructor stated that after the engine was started, he realized that the wheel chocks were still in place and not been removed from the left main landing gear. The flight instructor told the new student pilot to press the brake pedals with his feet while got out and removed the chocks. After the flight instructor climbed out of the airplane, it started to roll forward and impacted a hangar, resulting in substantial damage to the right wing's leading edge. The flight instructor stated that there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures of the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260708203350.s: A flight instructor and student pilot were involved when the aircraft rolled forward and struck a hangar after the instructor exited to remove wheel chocks while the student held the brakes. The incident caused substantial damage to the right wing's leading edge, with no preimpact mechanical failures reported.

NTSB:20260708203352.n: On July 7, 2026 about 1430 Alaska daylight time, a Piper PA-18-150 airplane, N824JT, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Mekoryuk, Alaska. The pilot and one passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 135, on-demand charter flight. The airplane, owned and operated by Renfro's Alaskan Adventures, departed from the Mekoryuk airport (MYU) at 1321 to conduct aerial game surveys for the Alaska Department of Fish and Game. About 1 hour and 10 minutes into the flight, about 200 ft. above the ground (agl) the engine began to run rough. The pilot applied carburetor heat, switched the fuel selector to both and began using different power settings. The engine initially began to run normally but subsequently loss partial power. The pilot elected to make a precautionary landing to the tundra, but while on final approach, all engine power was lost. The airplane touched down wings level and a slight nose up pitch. The landing gear separated from the fuselage and the airplane slid to a stop. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage and wings. A wreckage examination is pending recovery of the wreckage.
NTSB:20260708203352.s: The pilot of a Piper PA-18-150 conducting a Part 135 aerial survey near Mekoryuk, Alaska, experienced partial then total engine power loss at 200 feet AGL. The subsequent precautionary landing on tundra resulted in landing gear separation and substantial damage to the fuselage and wings, though occupants were uninjured.

NTSB:20260708203353.n: Before departing, the pilot found that the airplane's battery was "low," so he connected it to a charger for 15 minutes, after which he was able to start the engine normally. He subsequently completed three flight legs uneventfully, and was returning to his home airport when the accident occurred. As the pilot approached the destination airport, he noted that there was a thunderstorm in the area and elected to perform a downwind landing. During the landing approach, the pilot moved the landing gear position lever to the down position and extended the flaps. Due to the position the position of an electronic flight bag device in the cockpit, he did not observe that the landing gear down position indicator had not illuminated, nor did he realize that the landing gear circuit breaker had tripped. The pilot subsequently landed the airplane with the landing gear retracted, which resulted in substantial damage to the underside of the airplane's fuselage. Postaccident testing of the airplane's landing gear revealed that it functioned normally when external electrical power was applied, and that the landing gear position indication lights operated normally. Functional testing of the airplane's alternator and ammeter revealed that they functioned normally, but that the airplane's battery had little to no capacity due to having dead cells. It is likely that the battery's degraded condition resulted in the tripped landing gear system circuit breaker during the accident flight, and resulted in the landing gear's failure to extend. Had the pilot noticed that the landing gear did not extend as expected, he could have taken additional troubleshooting steps rather than continuing the landing with the landing gear not extended.
NTSB:20260708203353.s: The pilot landed a single-engine airplane with the gear retracted after failing to notice a tripped circuit breaker caused by a degraded battery. This resulted in substantial fuselage damage, as the battery's dead cells prevented gear extension despite normal alternator function.

NTSB:20260708203354.n: The pilot reported that, during landing, the airplane touched down and bounced. The pilot initiated a go-around; however, the airplane did not establish a positive rate of climb and subsequently bounced on the runway several more times. The airplane then ground-looped, exited the runway, and struck a drainage ditch, which resulted in the collapse of both main landing gear. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage and left-wing spar. The pilot reported no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation of the airplane. The pilot estimated that at the time of the accident, density altitude was greater than 8,000 ft.
NTSB:20260708203354.s: During landing in high density altitude, the pilot bounced, attempted a go-around, and ground-looped after failing to establish a positive climb. The aircraft exited the runway, struck a ditch, and collapsed both main landing gear, sustaining substantial damage with no reported mechanical failures.

NTSB:20260708203355.n: On July 7, 2026, about 1200 Pacific daylight time, a Luscombe 8A, N45886, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Novato, California. The pilot and passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. While conducting touch-and-go takeoff and landings on runway 31 at Gnoss Field (DVO), Novato, California, the engine experienced a partial loss of power during the departure climb about 600 ft above ground level. As the pilot attempted to return to the departure runway, he applied carburetor heat and the engine briefly regained power before experiencing a total loss of power. The pilot then moved the fuel selector from the wing tanks to the fuselage tank; however, he was unable to restart the engine. Subsequently, the airplane touched down in an area of soft gravel about 10 ft short of runway 13, and the left main landing gear collapsed. The airplane slid about 20 ft before it came to rest upright. Post accident examination of the airplane revealed that both wings sustained substantial damage. The airplane was recovered for further examination.
NTSB:20260708203355.s: During a touch-and-go departure from Gnoss Field, a Luscombe 8A suffered partial then total engine power loss at 600 feet. The pilot attempted a return landing but the left main gear collapsed upon touchdown in soft gravel, causing substantial damage to both wings.

NTSB:20260709203358.n: According to the pilot, during approach to the airport, he noted that the airplane felt "heavy and sluggish." The pilot realized the airplane was nearing its stall speed and low on its glidepath, and he attempted to correct by adding engine power and raising the nose; however, the airplane subsequently stalled and impacted terrain short of the runway. As a result, the airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage and the pilot received serious injuries. The pilot reported there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260709203358.s: During approach, the pilot reported the aircraft felt heavy and sluggish, leading to a stall and terrain impact short of the runway after attempting to correct low speed and glidepath. The pilot sustained serious injuries and the fuselage suffered substantial damage, with no pre-accident mechanical failures reported.

NTSB:20260709203360.n: The pilot of the tailwheel-equipped airplane reported that the airplane veered to the right during the landing roll. The pilot attempted to correct by applying left rudder and retracting the wing flaps; however, the airplane ground looped to the right. During the ground loop, the airplane's left wing and horizontal stabilizer impacted the runway surface, which resulted in substantial damage to the left wing, left elevator and horizontal stabilizer. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunction or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. At the time of the accident, the pilot was landing on runway 14 with light and variable wind.
NTSB:20260709203360.s: The pilot of a tailwheel-equipped airplane ground looped to the right while landing on runway 14 in light, variable winds. The incident caused substantial damage to the left wing, elevator, and horizontal stabilizer, with no preaccident mechanical failures reported.

NTSB:20260709203361.n: The accident flight was the non-certificated pilot's first flight in the unregistered airplane since he had overhauled the experimental engine. The pilot, who was also not certificated as a mechanic, performed the engine overhaul and subsequently conducted more than 5 hours of engine ground runs. During the initial climb after takeoff, the pilot observed an exhaust gas temperature of about 1,200°F. In response, he reduced engine power and initiated a right turn with the intention of re-entering the airport traffic pattern. At about 150 ft above ground level, the engine seized and experienced a total loss of power. The pilot conducted a forced landing straight ahead to a plowed field. During the landing roll, the main landing gear dug into the soft terrain, and the airplane nosed over. The empennage subsequently separated from the fuselage resulting in substantial damage. Following the accident, the pilot removed the wreckage from the accident site and disposed of it before the airframe and engine could be examined by investigators. The pilot did not possess a current FAA medical certificate. The pilot thought the airplane operated under Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 103 as an ultralight, however the airplane carried more than one person.
NTSB:20260709203361.s: A non-certificated pilot flying an unregistered experimental aircraft experienced total engine power loss at 150 feet after an engine overhaul, forcing a landing that resulted in a nose-over and empennage separation. The pilot disposed of the wreckage before investigation and lacked a current medical certificate, despite operating the multi-occupant aircraft as an ultralight.

NTSB:20260709203362.n: On July 8, 2026, at 1148 eastern daylight time, a Mooney M20 airplane was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Tallahassee, Florida. The pilot sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the pilot, the airplane had recently been sold, and he had been hired to ferry it from Florida to Texas. Prior to the flight, a known mechanical issue existed with the No. 5 cylinder. During the flight, the engine began surging, prompting the pilot to divert to Tallahassee International Airport (TLH), Tallahassee, Florida. While on the approach to TLH, about 1,000 feet mean sea level, all engine power was lost. The airplane subsequently impacted heavily wooded terrain about one-half mile short of Runway 18. According to a Federal Aviation Administration inspector that traveled to the scene, about 14 gallons of fuel were recovered from the wreckage following the accident. The airplane and engine have been recovered and retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260709203362.s: A pilot ferrying a Mooney M20 with a known No. 5 cylinder issue diverted to Tallahassee International Airport due to engine surging. The aircraft lost all power at 1,000 feet MSL during approach and impacted wooded terrain half a mile short of Runway 18, sustaining substantial damage and minor pilot injuries.

NTSB:20260710203363.n: Malta Air, doing business as Ryanair flight 1879, a Boeing 737-8AS, registration 9H-QEU, experienced a No. 2 (right) engine fan-blade-out (FBO) failure during climb out from the Thessaloniki International Airport (SKG), Thessaloniki, Greece. Engine fragments breached the fuselage and the cabin depressurized. The crew elected to return to SKG where they made an uneventful landing. The flight was a scheduled international passenger flight from SKG to Memmingen Airport (FMM), Memmingen, Germany. There were 2 pilots, 4 flight attendants, and 149 passengers (including one lap child) on board. One passenger sustained serious injuries. The NTSB traveled to the accident site. On July 16, 2026, the Greece Hellenic Air and Railway Safety Investigation Authority (HARSIA) delegated the investigation in full to the NTSB. As part of the investigative process, the NTSB invited qualified parties to participate in the investigation. These included the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), The Boeing Company, and GE Aerospace. In accordance with the provisions of Annex 13 to the Convention on International Civil Aviation, the countries of Greece (State of Occurrence), Malta (State of the Operator and Registry), and France (State of Manufacture of the Engines, jointly with the United States) designated Accredited Representatives to the investigation, and Malta Air, Safran Aircraft Engines, and the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) were designated as technical advisors. The parties were formed into specialized investigative groups led by NTSB group chairs in the areas of Powerplants, Structures and Survival Factors, and Materials Engineering. The Cockpit Voice Recorder (CVR) and Flight Data Recorder (FDR) were sent to NTSB headquarters for download and specialists were assigned. The materials engineer traveled to France to lead the engine fan blade examination. History of Flight According to the flight crew, while climbing through an altitude of about 16,000 ft, near Polykastro, Greece, (about 4.5 nm south of the Greek border with Northern Macedonia) they received a No. 2 engine HIGH VIBRATION indication. They reduced the engine power and initiated the Engine High Vibration non-normal checklist. Shortly after, the engine vibration indication was reduced. The crew subsequently continued the climb on autopilot. The engine vibrations then increased significantly, they heard a loud bang, and the autopilot was disengaged. While assessing the engine condition, the cabin altitude warning sounded. The flight crew donned their oxygen masks, declared an emergency, and began an immediate descent. The flight attendants (FAs), who were preparing for cabin service, reported hearing and feeling a loud continuous vibration and seeing a small amount of fog/smoke before the oxygen masks dropped. One reported hearing an automated public address system announcement saying “emergency descent”. Another recalled manually making an additional decompression announcement. The FAs recalled that passengers had donned their oxygen masks. FA2 and FA4 initially sat down in the forward jumpseats and donned their oxygen masks, however FA4 moved to the galley to use another mask after the one above the jumpseat detached from the overhead. FA1 noticed some passengers were standing up and asking for help and responded to assist. The FA noticed that the passenger in seat 11F was partially lodged in a damaged cabin window, and that the entire window was missing. Other passengers were assisting and managed to pull the injured passenger back into the cabin. The FA then sat in seat 11B and donned an oxygen mask. That mask became detached and the FA used a different one. A passenger went to the forward galley and asked the FA2 and FA4 for something heavy and metal to try and block the broken cabin window hole and retrieved a metal box to bring back to row 11. The injured passenger was subsequently moved to row 12 and was attended to by a passenger who was a doctor throughout the remainder of the flight. The doctor asked for first aid equipment, and FA1 retrieved the forward first aid kit. The FAs communicated with the flight deck, confirmed the flight crew were ok, and were informed of the engine failure, decompression, and the intent to return to SKG with an estimated time enroute of 20 minutes. The FAs also received instructions to secure the cabin, which they did. The flight crew later informed them when the oxygen masks were no longer necessary. After descending below 10,000 ft, the flight crew secured the No. 2 engine and returned to SKG uneventfully. The airplane remained on the runway for an inspection and then proceeded to the gate, where first responders were waiting. Figure 1: View of the row 11 passenger cabin window from the interior, right side of the cabin. Crew Experience The captain was hired by Malta Air in May 2015. He had accrued a total of 8,270 flight hours, 7,683 of which were in the same make and model as the accident airplane. The first officer was hired by Malta Air in March 2023. He had accrued a total of 2,523 flight hours, 2,333 of which were in the same make and model as the accident airplane. Airplane Examination Examination of the airplane revealed that the No. 2 engine, an CFM International (a joint company between Safran Aircraft Engines and GE Aerospace) model CFM56-7B26, experienced a fan blade separation that resulted in engine fragments striking the fuselage and the right horizontal stabilizer. The pressurized section of the fuselage was penetrated 1) through the passenger cabin window located at row 11, as well as 2) lower lobe fuselage skin behind the right wing-to-body fairing, see figures 2 and 3. Additional impact damage was found on the right wing-to-body fairing, a dent with paint smearing on the fuselage window belt skin, a dent on a stringer common to the dented fuselage window belt skin, a gouge on the right horizontal stabilizer upper skin and a dent on the right horizontal stabilizer leading edge. Figure 2: View of damage to right side of the fuselage. Figure 3: Fairing damage (left) and fuselage puncture behind fairing (right). Examination of the engine and nacelle revealed that one fan blade (No.10) had fractured and separated below the blade platform. The outer blade tips were fractured and separated on two additional fan blades (Nos. 16 and 21). All remaining blades were full length but exhibited varying levels of impact deformation. Three loose fan blade fragments were recovered from the engine. A visual examination of the core was performed and there was no evidence of radial uncontainment though the engine cases, or any undercowl fire. The engine inlet cowl, which is forward of the fan case, exhibited evidence of punctures as described below. The inlet and fan cowling remained attached to the engine. The inlet cowl inner barrel exhibited impact damage, tearing, and/or missing material from the 3 to 9 o’clock (as viewed from the rear) positions, see figure 4. The inlet lip skin had a scrape mark at approximately the 7 o’clock position. Figure 4: View of the No.2 (right) engine inlet. View is looking aft. The inlet cowl outer barrel had a radial penetration, forward of the fan plane of rotation at the 9:30 position that measured approximately 14 inches circumferentially by 10 inches axially. A second inlet cowl tear and puncture was present forward of the fan plane of rotation at the 7 o’clock position that measured approximately 13 inches circumferentially by 10 inches axially, see figure 5. Figure 5: No. 2 (right) engine inlet cowl outer barrel punctures. Several of the aft bulkhead splice fasteners failed at the 9:00, 6:00, and 3:00 o’clock positions. The attach ring to aft bulkhead fasteners failed 360 degrees circumferentially and loose rivet tails were observed along the bottom of the inner barrel. Enhancements for fasteners, defined in Federal Aviation Administration airworthiness directive (AD) 2025-04-01, had not been incorporated on this inlet cowl hardware. The inboard fan cowl sustained skin damage near the integrated drive generator (IDG) oil access door, and the No. 1 forward fan cowl latch was found disengaged after the event. The gap between the inboard fan cowl and thrust reverser was reduced at the bottom of the interface with contact observed at the forward edge of the thrust reverser. Enhancements for fasteners and an external doubler, defined in AD 2025-04-02, had not been incorporated on this fan cowl hardware. Bird remains, including feathers, were recovered from the forward face of IDG oil cooler, one of the thrust reverser blocker door drag links, and the lower (6 o’clock position) of the engine fan case near the thrust reverser split flange. The remains, along with the samples from the fan blades described below, were hand carried to the Smithsonian Institution Feather Identification Lab in Washington, DC, for examination. The exhaust nozzle remained attached to the engine. There was cracking and 360° shear buckling on the exhaust case immediately aft of the engine turbine rear frame. Enhancements for installing additional brackets for the exhaust nozzle, defined in AD 2025-04-03, had not been incorporated on this exhaust nozzle hardware. The FAA compliance date for all three of these ADs is July 2028. Fan Blades Examination Pieces from the fractured No.10 fan blade, the remaining 23 fan blades, and associated shims, spacers, and platforms were sent to Safran Aircraft Engines in Moissy-Cramayel, France for a group examination led by the Chief Technical Advisor for the NTSB Materials Laboratory, see figure 6 for relative location of shims, spacers and platforms to blades. Figure 6. Graphic showing location of blades, shims, spacers, and platforms. The red circle denotes location of the fracture on blade No. 10. (Source Safran Aircraft Engines, fracture area annotated by NTSB). The No. 10 fan blade was fractured through the dovetail in the blade root as shown in figure 7. A portion of the fracture surface covering approximately 37 percent of the total fracture surface had relatively smooth features with a curving boundary, features consistent with fatigue. The fracture features were traced back to an origin area on the concave side of the blade near the trailing edge. At the fatigue origin area located about 0.559 inch (14.2 mm) radially away from the root end face, ratchet marks were observed, consistent with multiple origins along an axial length of about 0.650 inch (16.5 mm). Heavy fretting damage was observed locally on the dovetail contact face adjacent to the origin area and in the same area on both sides of the associated shim. Figure 7. Fracture surface on the No. 10 fan blade dovetail piece (Source Safran Aircraft Engines). The fracture surface on the No. 10 fan blade dovetail piece was examined using a scanning electron microscope. The origin areas were damaged from fracture surface recontact and rubbing. However, fatigue striations were observed across the fatigue region from 0.008 inch (0.2 mm) deep to the boundary at a depth of 0.626 inch (15.9 mm). Striation spacing was relatively coarse and unchanged across the fatigue region, consistent with fracture due to high amplitude fatigue (HAF). In aircraft engine fan blade fractures, HAF is associated with cyclic loading that occurs at frequencies greater than a flight cycle and at stress amplitudes that are larger than those typically associated with high-cycle fatigue (HCF). The No. 10 spacer exhibited an area of elastomer deterioration near the trailing edge end, see figure 8. Figure 8. No. 10 spacer damage (Source Safran Aircraft Engines). Visual examinations were completed on the remaining 23 fan blades. Fan blade Nos. 8, 9, 12, and 21 had rounded deformation of the leading edges. The blades were further examined for evidence of organic material transfer using black light. Samples of fluorescing material were collected from blade Nos. 9, 11, 12, 20, 21, and an airfoil fragment from blade 10. Recorders An initial review of quick access recorder data revealed several evolutions of vibrations were detected by two sensors (one located at bearing No. 1, the other on the fan frame compressor case (FFCC)) for the No. 2 engine during take-off and climb. Vibration values for the FFCC sensor were higher than the bearing No.1 sensor during these phases and are provided below. The first was a sudden increase simultaneously from both sensors near the end of the take-off roll. The FFCC value increased from about 0.2 cockpit units (CU) to 1.7 CU before the airplane lifted off. The vibration value then rose from 1.7 to about 2.0 CU over the next 175 seconds. The rate of vibration change then increased, and the values rose from 2.0 CU to 4.3 CU over the next 250 seconds, until the engine power was reduced. As the power reduced, the vibration value decreased to about 1.2 CU. As the power was subsequently increased, the level rose first from 1.2 CU to 2.2 CU, then from 2.2 CU to the maximum recording limit of 5 CU within 19 seconds. The Honeywell solid state FDR readout is in progress at the NTSB Vehicle Recorder Laboratory. The airplane was equipped with a Honeywell solid state CVR that recorded the last two hours of aircraft operation across four channels. The event flight was about 57 minutes in duration and was captured in its entirety. Both English and Greek were spoken by the flight crew during the flight. Some cockpit discussions were not discernable because they were obscured by simultaneous radio transmissions. About seven and a half minutes after the start of the takeoff roll, the crew called for the high engine vibration non-normal checklist, noting that the vibration level was 4.3. No aural alert was audible on the CVR. A loud bang sound was recorded about nine minutes and twenty seconds after the start of the takeoff roll. The No.2 electronic engine control (EEC) unit and the airborne vibration monitor (AVM) unit were retained for data downloads at their respective manufacturers at a later date. Maintenance Records A review of maintenance records for the engine revealed that the fan blades had undergone ultrasonic inspections in accordance with CFM service bulletin (SB) 72-1033 revision 3, on November 11, 2025, and most recently on May 24, 2026, 253 cycles before the accident flight with no findings. It prescribes initial and recurring ultrasonic inspections of the concave and convex side of the fan blade dovetail, for any indications of crack development. The service bulletin was originally issued in 2018 following an FBO event in which a passenger was fatally injured. Four suspected bird strikes to the accident airplane’s No. 2 engine were reported by flight crews in the 12 months preceding the accident. No damage was found in the subsequent maintenance actions. Bird remains were reportedly found in two of the cases. Cabin Examination Examination of the airplane cabin revealed that the only emergency equipment found opened and used was a first aid kit found on seat 12F. All oxygen masks were found to be deployed. The forward flight attendant seat restraints were found all buckled, and aft flight attendant seat restraints were found unbuckled. All galley bins located in the forward and aft R1 were found stowed. Some of the locks and latches on the galley carts and bins were found in the unlatched position. The metal box mentioned in the flight attendant statement was found in the R1 aft galley, inboard second to the top compartment with no notable damages. Middle and outer passenger windowpane shards were found in the cabin area longitudinally between passenger rows 8 and 15. The interior sidewall panel surrounding the damaged passenger window at row 11, had a fracture at the lower aft vertical edge of the window that extended aft, to the nearest fuselage frame aft of the window edge. Additional Investigation Notes The No. 2 engine, along with its inlet, the No. 1 engine fan blades, shims and spacers, and the row 11 passenger window forging were retained for the investigation. The investigative team is aware of previous FBO events with similar engine models that resulted in damage to engine inlets or cowlings and fuselage structures. Determination of any relevant similarities or details between this accident and previous events remains under investigation. This investigation is ongoing.
NTSB:20260710203363.s: Malta Air flight 1879, a Boeing 737-8AS, suffered a No. 2 engine fan-blade-out during climb from Thessaloniki, causing fuselage penetration, depressurization, and one serious passenger injury. The crew returned to Thessaloniki for an uneventful landing after the blade separation breached the cabin window and damaged the horizontal stabilizer.

NTSB:20260710203364.n: On July 9, 2026, at about 2248 central daylight time, a Beech 95-B55, N202DK, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Waterloo, Illinois. The pilot and pilot rated passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. Family of the pilot reported that he had departed St. Louis Regional Airport (ALN) Alton/St. Louis, Illinois, on July 9 with an intended destination of Smith Field Airport (SLG), Siloam Springs, Arkansas. A family member, who was monitoring the airplane’s progress on a flight tracking application, saw the airplane stopped transmitting position data partway through the flight. The family member became concerned that the airplane may have crashed and subsequently notified local law enforcement. The FAA issued an Alert Notice (ALNOT) shortly after. The wreckage was located by Search and Rescue personnel the morning of July 10. There are no known witnesses to the accident sequence. Local law enforcement reported that on the night of the accident, the area experienced a significant storm with heavy rain, lightning, strong wind, and low visibility. Recorded ADS-B data showed that at 2226:06, the airplane departed from ALN on a southeast heading and climbed to altitude of about 3,800 ft mean sea level (msl). At 2238:28 the flight track data showed the airplane made a right turn to a southern heading and climbed to an altitude of about 5,000 ft msl. At 2240:54 the airplane made a right turn to a southwest heading and maintained an altitude of about 5,000 ft msl. At 2246:08 the airplane made a right turn to a western heading and descended to an altitude of about 4,500 ft msl. At 2247:41 the airplane made a left turn to the south and descended to about 4,100 ft msl. At 2247:57, while on a southern heading, the airplane climbed to an altitude of about 5,600 ft msl and its ground speed slowed to about 22 knots. At 2248:13, the data showed that the airplane initiated a descent, which continued until ADS-B contact was lost about 1,000 ft northwest of the accident site at 2248:40. Figure 1: ADS-B flight track. Examination of the accident site revealed that airplane’s wreckage came to rest in a field bisected by a line of trees about 4 miles southeast of Waterloo, Illinois. The tree line was orientated in a north / south direction and was about 30 ft wide with tree heights between 45 and 60 ft. The first identifiable point of contact (FIPC) was a ground scar that was about 8 ft in length and 30 ft in width. The debris path was oriented on a true heading of about 130° and was about 330 ft in length. The debris path extended through the tree line into an open grass field adjacent to the FIPC. The main wreckage was located about 50 ft from the FIPC within the tree line. Throughout the debris path, various portions of wing fragments, fuselage fragments, left engine, propeller blades, propeller hub fragments, and ailerons were observed. Additionally, several trees were damaged throughout the debris path. All major structural components of the airplane were located at the accident site. The wreckage was recovered to a secure location for further examination.
NTSB:20260710203364.s: A pilot and pilot-rated passenger were fatally injured when their Beech 95-B55 crashed near Waterloo, Illinois, during a Part 91 flight in severe storm conditions. ADS-B data showed the aircraft descended and slowed before impact, with wreckage found in a tree line following a debris path oriented on a 130° heading.

NTSB:20260710203365.n: On July 10, 2026, about 0745 eastern daylight time, a Sikorsky S-76D helicopter, N93RT, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Huntersville, West Virginia. The commercial pilot was fatally injured. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 positioning flight. The pilot of the helicopter departed a private hangar near Glenville, West Virginia about 0710 to pick up the helicopter’s owner at his property. Preliminary ADS-B data showed the helicopter flying from near the departure point directly toward the destination landing zone until it was about 0.5 nautical miles (nm) northwest of the destination when the helicopter made a right turn.
