The pilot reported that there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260717203416.s: During landing, the pilot reported the airplane porpoised, causing nose gear collapse, a runway excursion, and an inverted nosed-over stop. The pilot stated no preimpact mechanical malfunctions occurred, yet the fuselage, vertical stabilizer, and rudder sustained substantial damage.

NTSB:20260720203417.n: According to the pilot, he completed a preflight inspection but did not visually check the fuel quantity. Instead, he assumed the fuel was "at the tabs." While completing the cockpit checklist he noted that the fuel gauges indicated about three-quarters full, but he did not check them again during the flight. After takeoff, the pilot climbed to 9,500 ft mean sea level to avoid reported turbulence below 5,000 ft. During the flight, he switched between the fuel tanks when prompted by his yoke-mounted GPS. He reported that personal matters and cellphone use distracted him. When the fuel in the right tank was depleted, he turned toward the nearest airport. The fuel in the left tank was then depleted, the engine lost power, and the pilot began an emergency descent. During the descent, the pilot identified a logging road for a forced landing. He was initially too high and made a left circling turn to line up with the road. The airplane struck trees and came to rest next to the road. The right wing and fuselage sustained substantial damage.
NTSB:20260720203417.s: The pilot, distracted by personal matters and failing to visually verify fuel, experienced engine power loss after both tanks depleted during cruise at 9,500 ft. He attempted a forced landing on a logging road but struck trees, causing substantial damage to the right wing and fuselage.

NTSB:20260720203418.n: On July 19, 2026 about 1440 Alaska daylight time, a DeHavilland DHC-2 airplane, N791PW was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Nondalton, Alaska. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 business flight. The pilot reported that he conducted a normal landing on a remote airstrip, and after touching down he applied the brakes, but the right brake did not respond. The airplane veered to the left, the pilot attempted to correct the left drift by adding additional right brake; the brake did not respond. The airplane ground looped and departed the runway which resulted in substantial damage to the right wing and right elevator. A postaccident examination of the brake system is pending.
NTSB:20260720203418.s: The pilot of a DeHavilland DHC-2, N791PW, reported that the right brake failed to respond during landing at a remote airstrip near Nondalton, Alaska. The aircraft ground looped and departed the runway, causing substantial damage to the right wing and elevator while the pilot remained uninjured.

NTSB:20260720203420.n: The pilot reported that the density altitude was about 11,000 ft mean sea level when he departed and the airplane entered a climb. While approaching mountainous terrain east of the airport, the airplane began descending and the pilot was unable to maintain altitude. The pilot decided that it would be unsafe to turn back to his departure airport and decided to initiate a forced landing in a grass field between trees. The airplane impacted terrain during the landing attempt, which resulted in substantial damage to the wings and empennage. The pilot reported no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260720203420.s: The pilot departed an airplane at 11,000 ft density altitude and could not maintain altitude while climbing over mountainous terrain. He executed a forced landing in a grass field, resulting in substantial damage to the wings and empennage with no reported mechanical failures.

NTSB:20260720203421.n: The pilot reported that he performed four practice landings at the departure airport, to confirm landing performance, then continued to a private gravel airstrip. He overflew the airstrip and observed calm wind conditions, then performed another flyover to verify the runway was clear of obstructions. While on final approach, a gust of wind resulted in a temporary increase in airspeed then a touchdown farther than planned. After landing, during a "fast-taxi maneuver" he struck ground equipment that was obscured because of the tailwheel airplane's nose-high pitch attitude. The landing gear collapsed, then the airplane then struck another piece of equipment, which resulted in substantial damage to the left wing. The pilot stated that there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures of the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260720203421.s: The pilot of a tailwheel airplane struck obscured ground equipment during a fast-taxi maneuver after landing on a private gravel airstrip. A gust of wind caused a long touchdown, leading to landing gear collapse and substantial left wing damage, with no preimpact mechanical failures reported.

NTSB:20260720203422.n: The pilot reported that he filled the airplane with about 100 pounds of fuel and then initiated a take-off. After becoming airborne, a gust of wind hit the airplane from the left. The pilot stated the airplane stalled and dropped about 10 to 15 feet to the grass area next to the runway. The airplane then rolled about 20 to 30 ft, struck an earth berm at a taxiway, and nosed over, which resulted in substantial damage to the right wing, fuselage, and rudder. The pilot attributed the aerodynamic stall to the combination of increased takeoff weight after fueling, a 10,700 ft density altitude condition, and the gusting crosswind. The pilot reported there were no mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260720203422.s: The pilot reported that after fueling, a gusting crosswind caused an aerodynamic stall during takeoff at 10,700 ft density altitude. The aircraft dropped, struck an earth berm, and nosed over, resulting in substantial damage to the right wing, fuselage, and rudder.

NTSB:20260720203423.n: The pilot of the amphibious float equipped airplane reported that he was on a cross-country return flight to his home airport. During the descent to the planned fuel-stop airport, he encountered stronger headwinds than usual. The pilot closely monitored the fuel sight gauges because he recognized that the remaining fuel would be marginal for reaching his intended destination. While on a straight-in approach, positioned about 2 miles from the airport, the engine experienced a total loss of power. The pilot raised the airplane's nose to improve glide performance and engine power briefly returned; however, the engine subsequently lost total power a second time. The pilot retracted the landing gear and conducted a forced landing to a field. During the landing roll, the airplane struck a fence and came to rest nose-down in a ditch, resulting in substantial damage to both wings. The pilot reported that the engine lost power due to fuel exhaustion and that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260720203423.s: The pilot of an amphibious float-equipped airplane experienced total engine power loss twice during a straight-in approach due to fuel exhaustion. He executed a forced landing in a field, striking a fence and sustaining substantial wing damage, with no pre-accident mechanical failures reported.

NTSB:20260720203426.n: On July 18, 2026, about 1440 central daylight time, a Robinson Helicopter Company R44, N484AT, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Adair, Iowa. The pilot was not injured. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 137 aerial application flight. The pilot stated that he was recently hired by the owner to complete agricultural spraying operations. He spoke with the pilot who flew the helicopter on the previous day and reported that the engine governor was slow to respond and that he should watch it during subsequent flights. The accident pilot decided to load the helicopter with water and complete a test flight to ensure normal operations and no governor malfunctions. The test flight was completed with no anomalies noted, and the governor was working normally. The pilot completed about 5 hours of flight time and sprayed about 600 acres without incident. Shortly before the accident, the pilot landed the helicopter on the refueler truck and added 1 quart of oil to the engine, then continued to spray another field. The pilot had completed 2 to 3 spray passes and climbed out of the field to turn around for another pass. During the turn, the low rotor rpm horn sounded so the pilot lowered the collective and increased the throttle, which increased the rotor rpm and the horn turned off. The pilot continued another spray pass and the low rotor rpm horn sounded again. He attempted to increase the throttle beyond the governor limitation, but the horn continued. The helicopter was flying about 60 mph and was about 15 to 20 ft above the field, so he executed an autorotation and landed in the mature corn. The helicopter slid in the field and rolled left, then came to rest upright. The responding FAA inspector reported that the helicopter sustained substantial damage to the main rotor blades, fuselage, and tailcone. Postaccident examination revealed that the governor control unit was not secured to its mounting location but was still connected to the airframe main wiring harness. The owner and company mechanic stated that the helicopter was recently purchased for the agricultural business and discovered that the previous owner had removed the governor control unit. They acquired another governor control unit and helicopter underwent an overhaul. When the helicopter was put back into service, the governor control unit was not secured to its mounting location. The helicopter was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260720203426.s: A pilot flying a Robinson R44 during agricultural spraying encountered repeated low rotor rpm warnings caused by an unsecured governor control unit. The pilot executed an autorotation into a cornfield, resulting in substantial damage to the helicopter, though the pilot was not injured.

NTSB:20260720203427.n: On July 18, 2026, about 1530 Pacific daylight time, a Piper PA-28-161, N8249B, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near San Bernardino, California. The pilot and pilot rated passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported that while taxiing to the run-up area in preparation for takeoff at San Bernardino International Airport (SBD), San Bernadino, California, the airplane's right main landing gear collapsed, and the right wing impacted the taxiway surface. Postaccident examination of the airplane revealed that the right wing was substantially damaged. The airplane was recovered for further examination.
NTSB:20260720203427.s: The pilot of a Piper PA-28-161 reported that the right main landing gear collapsed while taxiing to the run-up area at San Bernardino International Airport. This caused the right wing to impact the taxiway, resulting in substantial damage to the aircraft, though the pilot and passenger were uninjured.

NTSB:20260721203428.n: The report provided by the company representative stated that the loader signaled to the helicopter pilot a thumbs up and walked down the stairs of the mobile loading platform. As the pilot was taking off, everything initially seemed normal until the pilot felt a tug on the helicopter. The helicopter pulled down and to the right and descended until it impacted the terrain in a right-side nose down attitude which resulted in substantial damage to the fuselage, tail boom, and main rotor. After the accident it was noted that the dry break coupler had broken off the refueling hose from the mobile loading platform and remained attached to the helicopter. The company representative reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the helicopter that would have precluded normal operation. When interviewed, the owner stated that the pilot was supposed to receive a thumbs-up or thumbs-down to indicate if the helicopter was ready to leave the platform. He also said the pilot was also supposed to visually verify that the fuel and chemical hoses were disconnected. The pilot stated he took off the moment he saw the loader walk down the stairs and made no mention of looking for a thumbs up from the loader. The loader did not remember if he signaled the pilot with a thumbs up indicating that it was safe to take off.
NTSB:20260721203428.s: A helicopter pilot took off from a mobile loading platform after seeing a loader descend stairs, but the aircraft impacted terrain when a dry break coupler remained attached to the refueling hose. The accident caused substantial damage, and the pilot failed to visually verify hose disconnection or receive a thumbs-up signal.

NTSB:20260721203430.n: The pilot reported that while giving rides, the airplane touched down and the right main landing gear contacted taller grass adjacent to the runway. The airplane ground looped to the right and exited the right side of the runway. During the ground loop, the left wing and elevator struck the ground. The airplane subsequently nosed over and came to rest inverted, which resulted in substantial damage to the upper and lower left wing, left elevator, and empennage.
NTSB:20260721203430.s: The pilot reported that while giving rides, the airplane's right main gear contacted tall grass, causing a ground loop and runway exit. The left wing and elevator struck the ground, resulting in the aircraft nosing over inverted with substantial damage to the left wing, elevator, and empennage.

NTSB:20260721203431.n: The pilot reported that while he was on approach, a communication with the air traffic control (ATC) tower controller interrupted his completion of the before landing checklist. The pilot reported that he forgot to resume the checklist and lower the landing gear. About 20 ft above the runway, the ATC controller alerted the pilot that his landing gear was retracted. The pilot applied full engine power and attempted to lower the landing gear; however, the airplane touched down on the runway without the landing gear properly configured, which resulted in substantial damage to the left wing and left aileron. The pilot did not submit the National Transportation Safety Board Pilot/Operator Aircraft Accident/Incident Report Form 6120.1.
NTSB:20260721203431.s: During approach, a pilot's before-landing checklist was interrupted by ATC, causing him to forget to lower the landing gear. After ATC alerted him at 20 feet, the aircraft touched down with gear retracted, resulting in substantial damage to the left wing and aileron.

NTSB:20260721203432.n: On July 16, 2026, about 1508 central daylight time, a Piper PA-24-260 airplane, N8606P, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Baraboo, Wisconsin. The pilot sustained serious injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported that for the cross-country flight, the airplane had about 6.5 hours of fuel onboard, and the planned flight only required about 2.5 hours of fuel. A preliminary review of ADS-B data showed the airplane depart, about 1232, from the Mitchell Municipal Airport (MHE), Mitchell, South Dakota. The airplane traveled to the east toward the destination airport, the Baraboo/Wisconsin Dells Regional Airport (DLL), Baraboo, Wisconsin. About 22 miles to the west of DLL, the pilot maneuvered the airplane to the south of DLL. About 17 miles to the south of DLL, the pilot maneuvered the airplane to the north toward DLL. According to air traffic control, the airplane was cleared for the RNAV (GPS) runway 1 instrument approach at DLL. As the airplane flew toward the approach end of runway 1, the airplane turned slightly to the west and then flew to the north over the various hangars, located to the west of runway 1. The airplane then maneuvered to the east, flying over runway 1. The pilot reported that the engine was not responding to his commands, but he did not hear any sputtering or popping noises. The airplane flew to the north of runway 1, the airplane turned to the west, and impacted trees. The pilot reported the airplane impacted trees because it could not produce climb power. The airplane came to rest upright on a flat grass field, on private property, located about 0.30 miles to the northwest of the approach end of runway 19. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage and to both wings. The airplane was recovered from the accident site, and it was transported to a secure location for future examination. A review of meteorological data from the closest weather reporting station, located at DLL, showed that the visibility at the time of the accident was about 1 3/4 miles, with moderate haze in the area, originating from large wildfires in Minnesota and Canada.
NTSB:20260721203432.s: The pilot of a Piper PA-24-260 sustained serious injuries when the aircraft impacted trees near Baraboo, Wisconsin, during an instrument approach. The pilot reported the engine failed to produce climb power despite no audible sputtering, causing the accident in moderate haze from wildfires.

NTSB:20260721203434.n: The pilot of the amphibious airplane reported that he was attempting to take off from a glassy water surface. The pilot had trouble getting the airplane "unstuck" from the water surface, so he pulled back on the control stick "extra hard." This action broke the floats free from the surface tension but created a nose-high pitch attitude that resulted in the airplane entering an aerodynamic stall. The left float then impacted the water and it broke loose from the airplane before striking the underside of the left wing, resulting in substantial damage to the left wing. The airplane came to rest upright but slowly began to sink. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260721203434.s: The pilot of an amphibious airplane stalled during takeoff from glassy water after pulling the control stick hard to break surface tension. The resulting nose-high attitude caused the left float to impact the water, break loose, and strike the left wing, causing substantial damage and sinking.

NTSB:20260721203436.n: On July 21, 2026, about 0815 mountain daylight time, an Enstrom F-28F helicopter, N8624B, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Malad City, Idaho. The pilot and pilot-rated passenger were not injured. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot in command, who was positioned in the left seat reported that the intent for the flight was to fly around the local area. After conducting a preflight inspection with no anomalies noted, he started the engine, conducted engine runup checks, increased the engine and rotor RPM to 100 percent and ascended to a hover. While conducting the helicopters in ground effect hover checks, he noticed that the manifold pressure was high, but still in the green. The pilot air taxied from the hangar parking area to the north toward the taxiway intersection near the approach end of runway 35 and saw that the manifold pressure was abnormally high. He landed the helicopter on the asphalt ramp to assess the instruments and conduct another magneto check, but when he rolled the throttle to flight idle, the engine lost total power. The pilot stated that with the engine and rotor RPM still married, he immediately engaged the starter and the engine restarted, but he noticed smoke emanating from the right side of the engine compartment, and there were flames on the lower left side of the engine. He attempted to shut down the engine by pulling the fuel/air mixture control on the instrument panel to the idle cut off position, but the engine continued to operate. He then turned the ignition switch to the off position to no avail, and he engaged the manual fuel shut-off located between the pilot and passenger seat, but the engine continued to operate. Unable to shut down the engine, the pilot and the passenger egressed the helicopter and searched for a fire extinguisher. Unable to locate a fire extinguisher, they contacted first responders, remained a safe distance from the burning helicopter and waited for the fire department to extinguish the blaze. The wreckage has been recovered to a secure facility for further examination.
NTSB:20260721203436.s: The pilot and passenger of an Enstrom F-28F helicopter experienced an engine fire during ground operations after the engine lost power and restarted with smoke and flames. Despite multiple attempts to shut down the engine using mixture, ignition, and manual fuel controls, the pilot and passenger evacuated as the helicopter burned.

NTSB:20260721203439.n: The pilot reported that while on approach to the runway, he was distracted and failed to adjust his aimpoint for the short-field approach and landing. As the airplane touched down on the grass runway at about 70 miles per hour, he applied the brakes, however, the airplane's speed was too fast to stop before reaching the end of the runway. The nose of the airplane turned to the left, the airplane overran the end of the runway and came to rest on down sloping terrain in a drainage culvert beyond the runway threshold. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the engine mount and fuselage. The pilot reported no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. The pilot added that he had at that airport many times, and the uphill slope of the runway provided him with false confidence.
NTSB:20260721203439.s: The pilot, while on approach to a short-field grass runway, failed to adjust his aimpoint due to distraction. The aircraft overran the runway at 70 mph, sustaining substantial damage to the engine mount and fuselage after coming to rest in a drainage culvert.

NTSB:20260721203440.n: On July 20, 2026, about 1340 central daylight time, a Piper PA-28-180, N454MD was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Bulberde, Texas. The flight instructor and student pilot received minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 91 instructional flight. The flight instructor reported that they had been performing takeoff and landing practice and had accomplished three successful takeoffs and landings. On the forth takeoff, when the airplane was 50 to 60 ft above the ground, the engine stopped producing power. A forced landing was executed, during which, the airplane struck trees and sustained substantial damage to the fuselage, both wings, and the empennage surfaces. The airplane has been retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260721203440.s: During a Part 91 instructional flight in a Piper PA-28-180, the flight instructor and student pilot suffered minor injuries when the engine lost power at 50 to 60 feet during a fourth takeoff. The subsequent forced landing resulted in substantial damage to the fuselage, wings, and empennage after the aircraft struck trees.

NTSB:20260722203441.n: On his first solo flight in the glider, the pilot reported that while on final approach about 5-8 ft above the runway surface, he pulled back on the stick to flare. The glider pitched up and stalled and subsequently bounced hard, about three times before coming to a rest, causing substantial damage to the fuselage. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident malfunctions or failures with the glider that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260722203441.s: During his first solo glider flight on final approach, the pilot flared at 5-8 feet, causing the aircraft to pitch up, stall, and bounce three times. This resulted in substantial fuselage damage, with the pilot reporting no pre-accident malfunctions.

NTSB:20260722203442.n: The pilot reported that, while taxing from the ramp to the runway, he became distracted by a helicopter to the right and perpendicular to the airplane. While he observed the helicopter, the pilot inadvertently taxied into a grassy area and subsequently impacted a drainage pipe. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage. The pilot reported that there were no mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane prior to the accident.
NTSB:20260722203442.s: The pilot reported that while taxiing from the ramp to the runway, distraction by a helicopter caused the airplane to inadvertently enter a grassy area and impact a drainage pipe. This resulted in substantial fuselage damage, with no mechanical malfunctions reported prior to the accident.

NTSB:20260723203444.n: On July 20, 2026, at 1030 eastern daylight time, a Cessna 152 airplane was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Pell City, Alabama. The flight instructor and student pilot were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight. According to the instructor they departed St. Clair County Airport (KPLR), Pell City, Alabama, with full fuel tanks for a training flight. About four minutes after departure about 1,500 to 2,000 ft above ground level (agl), the engine lost all power and the instructor performed a forced landing to a field. After landing the airplane continued through a fence and the left wing impacted a tree. According to a Federal Aviation Administration inspector that traveled to the scene the left fuel tank was ruptured. The airplane was recovered and an engine test run was performed. The engine did not run smoothly, and the throttle had to be pumped to keep the engine running. The engine was shut down and secured for further examination.
NTSB:20260723203444.s: A flight instructor and student pilot in a Cessna 152 experienced total engine power loss at 1,500 to 2,000 feet agl during a Part 91 training flight. The subsequent forced landing resulted in substantial damage after the left wing struck a tree, with post-accident testing revealing a ruptured left fuel tank and rough engine operation.

NTSB:20260723203446.n: During an instructional flight, the flight instructor was demonstrating a landing. Upon touchdown, the flight instructor noticed that the airplane was right of centerline. He applied left rudder to realign the airplane with the centerline but overcorrected. The airplane veered sharply left, then he tried to correct with right rudder and the airplane veered sharply to the right. The airplane exited the runway surface and went through a ditch. The nose landing gear separated before the airplane slid through the grass and struck the concrete base of a tetrahedron. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the forward fuselage and wings. The flight instructor reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260723203446.s: During an instructional landing, the flight instructor overcorrected rudder inputs while realigning the aircraft, causing it to veer off the runway and strike a tetrahedron. The nose gear separated, resulting in substantial damage to the forward fuselage and wings, with no pre-accident mechanical failures reported.

NTSB:20260724203452.n: On July 20, 2026, at 0643 central daylight time, a Piper J3C-65 airplane, N92432, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Richmond, Texas. The commercial pilot sustained serious injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The airplane impacted the roof of a house near the airport traffic pattern for Covey Trails Airport, Richmond, Texas. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage and wings. The pilot stated that he did not remember the circumstances leading to and nature of the accident. Postaccident examination of the airplane confirmed flight control continuity from the cockpit flight controls to the respective flight control surfaces. The two-blade wood propeller and metal propeller spinner did not display torsional features consistent with engine power. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260724203452.s: A commercial pilot flying a Piper J3C-65 near Richmond, Texas, struck a house roof while operating under Part 91, sustaining serious injuries and substantial aircraft damage. The pilot had no memory of the event, and post-accident examination showed no engine power indications on the propeller.

NTSB:20260724203453.n: On July 23, 2026, about 1720 Pacific daylight time, a De Havilland DHC-3 Otter airplane, N709KA, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Eastsound, Washington. The pilot and two passengers were seriously injured, and eight passengers sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 135 scheduled air taxi flight. According to the operator, the flight originated from Kenmore Sea Base (W55), Seattle, Washington at 1630 with scheduled stops at Roche Harbor (WA03), Roche Harbor, Washington and Friday Harbor (W33), Friday Harbor, Washington. Preliminary ADS-B data showed that the airplane departed W55 about 1633 and maintained about 500 to 1,000 ft mean sea level (msl). The airplane remained over the water and generally travelled north over Rosario Strait. Once northwest of Lummi Island, the airplane turned west and passed north of Sucia Island. The operator stated that the pilot radioed the company operations center and reported inclement weather, which precluded the flight from continuing to WA03. The pilot informed the operator that he would return to Sucia Island, land, and wait for the weather to improve. The operator reported that there were multiple bays around Sucia Island where the pilot was authorized to land. ADS-B data showed that about 1619, when the airplane was about 11 miles northeast of WA03, it turned right about 180° and flew about 5 miles towards Sucia Island. Video imagery, from a witness who was near Shallow Bay, Sucia Island, showed the airplane at a low altitude and a nose-high attitude descending towards the water. When the airplane was about 4 ft above the water, the left wing dropped and the left wingtip and left pontoon float impacted the water. The airplane then landed with both pontoon floats on the water and continued forward where it subsequently impacted rocks. A passenger on the airplane reported that multiple small boats immediately arrived to remove the passengers from the accident site. A postaccident fire destroyed the fuselage after all passengers and the pilot had exited. The airplane was recovered to a secure hanger for further examination.
NTSB:20260724203453.s: A pilot flying a De Havilland DHC-3 Otter on a Part 135 air taxi flight attempted to land on water near Sucia Island due to inclement weather. The left wingtip and pontoon struck the water at 4 feet altitude, causing the aircraft to impact rocks and sustain substantial damage, followed by a post-accident fire.

NTSB:20260726203454.n: On July 24, 2026, about 1422 central daylight time, a Zenith Zodiac 601HDS experimental airplane, N27601, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Sioux City, Iowa. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The multi-leg visual flight rules (VFR) cross country flight departed from the Wittman Regional Airport (KOSH), Oshkosh, Wisconsin, with a final destination in Colorado. At 1236 on the day of the accident, ADS-B data showed the airplane departed the Pocahontas Municipal Airport (KPOH), Pocahontas, Iowa, on a southwesterly flight track. Upon reaching the vicinity of Holstein, Iowa, the airplane then flew west parallelling U.S. Highway 20 in the direction of Sioux City, Iowa. About 3 miles short of the U.S. Highway 20/75 intersection, the airplane began to track to the northwest, eventually turned north, and began climbing. After flying north, the airplane entered a right turn and descended until the last recorded data point which was located about a half mile southeast of the accident site. The airplane was found in about 6 to 8 feet of water in a man-made lake near the shoreline. The vegetation along the shoreline on the side of the accident site, as well as the bank opposite the accident site about 80 to100 feet away, was intact with no indication of having been struck by the accident airplane. The main wing spar remained intact along its length but from the main landing gear outward on both sides, the wing structure and wing skins showed aft crushing and had mostly separated from the spar. The fuselage was deformed 90° from the wing spar. The instrument panel, firewall, and engine separated from the front of the airplane and were located underneath and near the area the main wreckage came to rest. Upper engine cowling and windscreen fragments were scattered across the shoreline and a yard beyond the water. Divers and a local towing company were able to remove the airplane from the water. The major components of the airplane were present. Flight control cable continuity was established for the ailerons, rudder, and elevators. A visual inspection of the engine did not reveal any signs of a catastrophic engine failure. The wreckage was moved to a secure location for further examination. According to KPOH personnel, the pilot purchased 14.7 gallons of 100 low lead fuel before departing. At the accident site, fuel sheen was present on the water and oil was present in the water during the recovery of the engine. The National Weather Service (NWS) Area Forecast Discussion issued by the Sioux Falls, South Dakota, Weather Forecast Office at 1209 on the day of the accident reported instrument flight rules (IFR) to marginal instrument flight rules (MVFR) conditions would slowly improve through midafternoon. On the day of the accident around 1500, another pilot was flying west about 75 miles south of the accident pilot. He reported that conditions were worse than forecast, and he had to divert to avoid instrument meteorological conditions. He landed at an alternate airport and ended up driving home. A review of FAA records showed the pilot held a private pilot certificate with a rating for airplane single engine land, but no instrument rating. The pilot, who was the airplane owner, built the airplane and he held a repairman experimental aircraft builder certificate for the airplane.
NTSB:20260726203454.s: The private pilot of an experimental Zenith Zodiac 601HDS was fatally injured when the aircraft crashed into a lake near Sioux City, Iowa, during a VFR cross-country flight. The accident occurred in deteriorating weather conditions, with the pilot lacking an instrument rating and the aircraft sustaining structural separation upon impact.

NTSB:20260727203456.n: On July 22, 2026, about 1129 Pacific daylight time, an experimental amateur built Czech Aircraft Works Mermaid Skeeter 2 airplane, N42SK, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Cougar, Washington. The pilot was seriously injured. The airplane was operated under Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. A review of a video provided by a witness showed the airplane at a distance while flying at a low altitude, in a right banking turn. The airplane subsequently began to descend while in a right bank and impacted the water of Yale Lake. The airplane remained partially above water surface for an unspecified time before it ultimately became submerged. Recovery of the wreckage is currently pending.
NTSB:20260727203456.s: The pilot of an experimental Czech Aircraft Works Mermaid Skeeter 2, N42SK, was seriously injured when the aircraft impacted Yale Lake during a low-altitude right banking turn. The airplane was substantially damaged and submerged while operating under Part 91 personal flight rules.

NTSB:20260727203459.n: During a low-altitude aerial herbicide application along an electrical transmission right-of-way, the helicopter struck power lines. Following the wire strike, the helicopter impacted terrain and sustained substantial damage to the tailboom, main rotor, and fuselage. The pilot was seriously injured. The operator reported no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the helicopter that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260727203459.s: During a low-altitude aerial herbicide application, a helicopter struck power lines and impacted terrain, sustaining substantial damage to the tailboom, main rotor, and fuselage. The pilot was seriously injured, and the operator reported no preaccident mechanical malfunctions.

NTSB:20260727203460.n: The pilot reported that while attempting to land, the airplane touched down, encountered a right crosswind, and began to drift to the left. The pilot attempted to correct the movement by applying opposite rudder and subsequently increased engine power to attempt to go around. However, the left wing contacted the ground, and the airplane then impacted terrain. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the right wing, tail and empennage. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical failures or malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260727203460.s: During landing, the pilot encountered a right crosswind causing left drift and attempted a go-around with opposite rudder and increased power. The left wing contacted the ground, resulting in terrain impact and substantial damage to the right wing, tail, and empennage with no reported mechanical failures.

NTSB:20260727203461.n: The pilot reported that after touching down, smoothly on centerline, the airplane veered right. He attempted to apply corrective control inputs which were not successful. The airplane then began to slide, which resulted in the left main wheel and subsequently the right main wheel separating from the landing gear. The airplane continued to slide on the main landing gear struts, with the lower left wing dragging on the runway, until the airplane came to stop on the edge of the runway nearly, and oriented nearly perpendicular to it. This resulted in substantial damage to the lower left wing and aileron. Postaccident photographs showed a rubber witness mark on the right main landing gear strut and fractures of both the main landing gear wheel axles. Given this information, it is likely that during the touchdown sequence the right main landing gear wheel axle began to separate, which resulted in the right main wheel coming into contact with the right main landing gear strut. The contact with the right main landing gear strut likely resulted in the right uncorrectable motion the pilot reported and subsequent sideload and separation of both main landing gear.
NTSB:20260727203461.s: The pilot reported that after a smooth touchdown, the aircraft veered right uncontrollably, causing both main wheels to separate and the left wing to drag until stopping off the runway. Post-accident analysis suggests a right main gear axle fracture during touchdown caused the uncorrectable veer and subsequent gear separation.

NTSB:20260727203462.n: The pilot reported that during the landing flare, the airplane contacted the runway hard and bounced twice before he was able land and bring the airplane to a stop near the departure end of the runway. The airplane's lower fuselage was substantially damaged during the accident sequence. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260727203462.s: The pilot reported a hard landing and two bounces during the flare, resulting in substantial lower fuselage damage. No pre-accident mechanical malfunctions were identified that would have prevented normal operation.

NTSB:20260727203463.n: On July 26, 2026, at 1941 central daylight time, an experimental Kitfox III airplane, N573TB, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Ephraim, Wisconsin. The private pilot and a passenger were uninjured. The airplane was operated under Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations as a Part 91 personal flight. The pilot stated that he had flown the airplane for about an hour and was returning to Ephriam Airport, Ephraim, Wisconsin. During approach for landing on runway 14, the airplane engine suddenly lost total power. The pilot then performed a forced landing to a field about 3 miles east/northeast of the airport. The airplane sustained substantial damage to both wings. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260727203463.s: A private pilot flying an experimental Kitfox III, N573TB, experienced a total engine power loss during approach to runway 14 at Ephraim Airport. The pilot executed a forced landing in a nearby field, resulting in substantial damage to both wings, though both occupants remained uninjured.

NTSB:20260727203464.n: On July 27, 2026, about 0819 central daylight time, an Aero Commander Callair A-9B airplane, N7799V, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Livonia, Missouri. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 137 agricultural application flight. The pilot stated that he was spraying a field at the time of the accident. When the airplane was about 50 feet above ground level, the engine lost power abruptly as it came over a tree line on a final application pass. The pilot conducted a forced landing into the soybean field. The airplane sustained damage to the ailerons, fuselage, empennage and rudder during the forced landing. Figure 1 - Airplane at accident site he pilot informed investigators that the airplane was fully fueled before the flight. Examinations of the engine and airframe fuel system are planned following recovery of the airplane from the accident site.
NTSB:20260727203464.s: The pilot of an Aero Commander Callair A-9B operating a Part 137 agricultural flight reported abrupt engine power loss at 50 feet AGL while spraying. This forced a landing into a soybean field, substantially damaging the ailerons, fuselage, empennage, and rudder, though the pilot was uninjured.

NTSB:20260728203465.n: The flight instructor was providing instruction to the pilot toward a tailwheel endorsement. During their second flight of the day, the flight instructor demonstrated a normal traffic pattern and 3-point landing, after which the pilot flew the subsequent traffic pattern and landing approach. As the pilot attempted a 3-point landing, the airplane touched down with slight drift. The pilot attempted to correct the drift but applied excessive right and then left rudder control inputs. The airplane subsequently ground looped and sustained substantial damage to the right wing. The flight instructor reported that there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260728203465.s: A student pilot and flight instructor were conducting a tailwheel endorsement training flight when the student ground looped during a three-point landing attempt. Excessive rudder inputs while correcting drift caused the ground loop, resulting in substantial damage to the right wing with no mechanical failures reported.

NTSB:20260728203468.n: On July 23, 2026, at 1440 eastern daylight time, an American AA-1, N6132L, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Kearneysville, West Virginia. The pilot and pilot-rated passenger were seriously injured. The airplane was being operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. A review of ADS-B data showed that the airplane departed from Eastern West Virginia Regional Airport (MRB), Martinsburg, West Virginia at 1345 and proceed about 20nm south where it performed a series of maneuvers before flying back toward MRB. During a postaccident interview, the pilot stated that while he was descending the airplane from 3,000 ft to 1,500 ft to enter the airport traffic pattern, the engine suddenly lost all power. Unable to reach the airport, he elected to make an emergency landing in a field about 5 nm south of MRB. During the forced landing, the airplane's right wing and engine separated from the fuselage. The fuselage, left wing, and empennage were substantially damaged. The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260728203468.s: The pilot and passenger of an American AA-1, N6132L, were seriously injured when the engine lost all power during descent from 3,000 to 1,500 feet near Martinsburg, West Virginia. The pilot attempted an emergency landing in a field, resulting in the right wing and engine separating from the fuselage and causing substantial damage.

NTSB:20260728203470.n: On July 14, 2026, about 1725 Pacific daylight time, a Piper PA-24 airplane, N5002P, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident at Rogue Valley International/Medford Airport (MFR), Medford. Oregon. The two pilots were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The flight instructor reported that he and the pilot had intended to familiarize themselves with the airplane after it had been purchased by a new owner. Prior to the accident flight, the new airplane owner reported to the flight instructor that the prebuy inspection had identified some landing gear anomalies. Most of the anomalies were addressed during subsequent maintenance with exception of a delayed landing gear annunciation, which they were unable to duplicate. During the accident flight, one of the pilots asked the air traffic controller to observe if the landing gear was down. On the third circuit in the traffic pattern, the pilots heard the landing gear extend; however, the gear indication for the down and locked position did not illuminate. The pilot asked the tower controller to observe the landing gear position again, and the controller confirmed it was down. Nevertheless, about 200 ft - 300 ft above ground level, the landing gear down and lock position light illuminated and the pilot continued the approach and landing. Shortly after touchdown, during the landing roll, the landing gear collapsed and the airplane subsequently came to rest on the runway. Postaccident examination by a FAA inspector revealed that the engine mount sustained substantial damage. The airplane was recovered and retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260728203470.s: Two pilots operating a Piper PA-24 for personal flight experienced a landing gear collapse shortly after touchdown at Medford Airport. Despite visual confirmation from air traffic control that the gear was down, the gear failed during the landing roll, causing substantial damage to the engine mount.

NTSB:20260728203471.n: On July 24, 2026, about 1550 central daylight time, a Beech V35 airplane, N3707Q, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Carroll, Iowa. The pilot was not injured. The flight was operated under the provisions of Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 as a personal flight. According to the pilot, he departed from the Arthur N Neu Airport (CIN), Carroll, Iowa, and flew towards Stanton County Municipal Airport (JHN), Johnson City, Kansas. The pilot reported that shortly after takeoff, the engine started to run rough. He turned back towards CIN and noticed that the oil pressure began to decrease. About 5 miles from CIN, the oil pressure dropped to zero. When the airplane was about 3 miles from the airport, the engine started to smoke, and total engine power was lost. He performed a forced landing to a bean field. During the forced landing, the right aileron sustained substantial damage. A postaccident visual inspection of the engine revealed a hole in the crankcase above the No. 4 cylinder and additional case damage above the No. 3 cylinder. The oil dipstick showed little or no oil remained in the sump. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260728203471.s: The pilot of a Beech V35 experienced rough running and zero oil pressure shortly after takeoff, leading to total engine power loss and smoke. He performed a forced landing in a bean field, sustaining substantial damage to the right aileron due to an engine crankcase failure and oil loss.

NTSB:20260728203474.n: During a turn while taxiing near a fuel farm at a slow speed, the airplane's left wing contacted the fuel facility fence. Following the initial impact, the airplane pivoted toward the fence, resulting in additional contact with the fenced enclosure. The collision resulted in substantial damage to the left wing and fuselage. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. Following the accident, the pilot identified several areas to reduce the risk of similar occurrences. These areas included conducting a more deliberate visual assessment of obstacle clearance before initiating turns in confined ramp or taxi areas, requesting wing-walking assistance or external guidance when maneuvering near obstacles, and allowing additional taxi distance before beginning turns to increase wingtip clearance margins.
NTSB:20260728203474.s: The pilot reported that while taxiing near a fuel farm, the airplane's left wing struck a fence, causing substantial damage to the wing and fuselage. The pilot attributed the incident to insufficient obstacle clearance during the turn and noted no pre-accident mechanical failures.

NTSB:20260728203476.n: On July 27, 2026, about 2130 Alaska daylight time, a deregistered Piper PA-22-150 airplane, N4535A, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Chitina, Alaska. The pilot and two passengers were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to witnesses, the pilot and two passengers departed McCarthy Airport, McCarthy, Alaska, to drop off the passengers and supplies at the upper Dan Creek airstrip, located about 12 miles southeast of McCarthy. The upper Dan Creek airstrip is an uncharted private strip that is generally considered one way in and out, surrounded by steeply rising terrain, and go-arounds are not recommended. Multiple witnesses, located on the ground in the vicinity of the airstrip, reported hearing the airplane approaching the southeast runway for landing at a normal approach power setting. The witnesses stated that they then heard the airplane’s engine increase to a high-power setting, then there was a moment of silence, followed by the sound of an impact. The airplane impacted a berm on a rock-covered riverbank in a left-wing-low flight attitude about 740 ft north of the airstrip. The wreckage was oriented on a northwest heading. All four corners of the airplane were accounted for at the accident site. The outboard portion of the left wing was bent downwards and aft. The fuselage, inboard left wing, and portions of the inboard right wing were consumed by a postimpact fire. During the onsite investigation, no preimpact anomalies were visually observed with the flight control system. The fuel selector was positioned on the left tank, and 100LL aviation fuel was present in the left wing. The throttle was found in the idle position and was bent in the direction of the pilot. The propeller blades exhibited rotational signatures including leading edge tip damage and chordwise witness marks, indicative of operation at a low-power setting upon impact. The engine has been recovered to a secure facility for further examination.
NTSB:20260728203476.s: A Piper PA-22-150 carrying a pilot and two passengers crashed near Chitina, Alaska, while attempting to land at an uncharted airstrip. The aircraft impacted a riverbank in a left-wing-low attitude after witnesses heard the engine power increase, resulting in fatalities and a post-impact fire.

NTSB:20260728203478.n: The pilot of the tailwheel equipped airplane reported that he was preparing the airplane for landing and the landing gear would not extend. He attempted to extend the landing gear using the airplane's manual gear extension procedure and during that effort, the fuel selector valve was inadvertently moved to the OFF position rather than the hydraulic system depressurization valve. The engine experienced a total loss of power, and the pilot initiated a forced landing to a field, resulting in substantial damage to the left wing and fuselage. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260728203478.s: The pilot of a tailwheel airplane attempted manual gear extension during landing preparation but inadvertently moved the fuel selector to OFF instead of the hydraulic depressurization valve. This caused total engine power loss, forcing a field landing that resulted in substantial damage to the left wing and fuselage.

NTSB:20260729203480.n: On July 28, 2026, about 1949 mountain standard time, a Piper PA-28-180, N9062J, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Chandler, Arizona. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. Preliminary ADS-B data obtained from a commercially available source showed that the airplane departed runway 22R at Chandler Municipal Airport (CHD), Chandler, Arizona, at 1948:10. The airplane continued southwest on the departure leg and climbed to a reported GPS altitude of about 1,800 ft. The final recorded ADS-B point, at 1949:31, showed a reported ground speed of 45 knots and a descent rate of about 130 ft per minute. Witnesses at a park about 0.5 miles southeast of the accident site reported observing the airplane flying southwest when they heard the engine sound cease. They stated that the airplane then entered a sharp right turn and descended rapidly. A dashcam video provided to the NTSB depicted the airplane in a steep right bank and rapid descent before ground impact. The airplane impacted a commercial plumbing-supply yard about 0.7 miles from the departure end of runway 22L at CHD. The first identified impact point was a ground scar about 30 ft southwest of the main wreckage. The main wreckage was oriented on an approximate magnetic heading of 097° at an elevation of about 1,226 ft mean sea level. The forward fuselage rested on the concrete lot, while the aft fuselage and empennage extended across a curb into an adjacent dirt-and-gravel area. The engine, fuselage, cabin, wings, and empennage exhibited extensive thermal damage. The wreckage was recovered to a secure location for further examination.
NTSB:20260729203480.s: A pilot operating a Piper PA-28-180 on a Part 91 personal flight was fatally injured when the aircraft crashed near Chandler, Arizona, shortly after departing runway 22R. Witnesses and video reported the engine sound ceased, followed by a sharp right turn and rapid descent into a commercial yard.

NTSB:20260729203483.n: On July 24, 2026, about 14:32 Coordinated Universal Time, a Delta Air Lines Boeing 757-200, N662DN, powered by two Pratt & Whitney PW2037 turbofan engines, experienced a No. 1 (left) engine fire during initial climb from Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), Atlanta, Georgia. The captain and first officer (FO) were uninjured. The flight was operating under Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 as a non-scheduled, maintenance ferry flight from ATL to Querétaro Intercontinental Airport (QRO), Mexico. According to the flight crew, the pre-flight, taxi, and takeoff were uneventful. The captain was the pilot flying and the FO was the pilot monitoring. While climbing through 12,000 ft, a L ENG FIRE MASTER WARNING was displayed on the engine indicating and crew alerting system (EICAS) with an accompanying aural fire bell. The captain continued flying and the FO executed the engine fire checklist. The engine was successfully shutdown, one fire bottle was discharged, and the fire indication extinguished shortly thereafter. The crew declared an emergency, requested an immediate return to ATL, and performed an uneventful landing. The crew did not observe any additional cockpit fire indications after landing and elected to vacate the runway and taxi to a gate. Post-landing inspection by airport rescue and fire-fighting (ARFF) found sooting and thermal damage on the No. 1 engine and nacelle components, extending up toward the pylon structure. Subsequent inspection by Delta Airlines maintenance found a tear near the top of the outer diffuser case. Figure 1: External engine condition Figure 2: Top of outer diffuser case The NTSB invited qualified parties to participate in the investigation, including the Federal Aviation Administration, the Boeing Company, Delta Air Lines, and Pratt & Whitney. NTSB specialist support includes Flight Data Recorders and Powerplants.
NTSB:20260729203483.s: During a maintenance ferry flight, a Delta Boeing 757-200 experienced a left engine fire at 12,000 feet while climbing from Atlanta. The crew successfully shut down the engine and discharged a fire bottle, returning for a safe landing; post-flight inspection revealed a tear in the outer diffuser case.

NTSB:20260730203490.n: The pilot reported that while performing agricultural spray applications, a vehicle parked on the road in the vicinity of the field he was spraying. He made a 360° turn waiting for the vehicle to move. During the turn, the airplane lost airspeed and entered an aerodynamic stall. The pilot attempted to recover the airplane from the stall by pitching the nose of the airplane down and applying full power. However, during the recovery, the airplane entered a secondary aerodynamic stall. The airplane impacted power lines and trees and then impacted a residential yard. The fuselage, wings, and horizontal stabilizer were substantially damaged. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical failures or malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260730203490.s: During agricultural spray operations, a pilot stalled the aircraft while circling a parked vehicle. The plane entered a secondary stall during recovery, struck power lines and trees, and crashed into a residential yard, causing substantial damage with no reported mechanical failure.

NTSB:20260730203491.n: The flight instructor stated that he was taking the private pilot on a familiarization and training flight. The flight instructor planned to fly to a nearby turf runway where he would demonstrate a soft-field takeoff. While departing from the turf runway, the flight instructor flew the airplane in ground effect longer than was necessary and then turned left crosswind while still at a low altitude. The airplane's left wing subsequently contacted a barbed wire fence, and the wire wrapped around the wing. The flight instructor returned to the airport, landed uneventfully, and removed the barbed wire from the wing. He subsequently performed a preflight inspection, and after nothing that the flight control surfaces were operating normally, returned to the airplane's home airport uneventfully. Subsequent examination of the airplane revealed the left wing had been substantially damaged. The flight instructor reported that there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures of the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260730203491.s: A flight instructor and private pilot struck a barbed wire fence with the left wing during a low-altitude crosswind turn after a soft-field takeoff demonstration. The instructor landed, removed the wire, and returned home, though the wing sustained substantial damage with no mechanical failure reported.

NTSB:20260802203499.n: On August 1, 2026, about 2301 mountain daylight time (MDT), a Cessna 172G, N1166F, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Blackfoot, Idaho. The pilot was fatally injured, and the two passengers sustained serious injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. A witness reported the pilot completed 3 takeoffs and landings for night currency before departing on the accident flight about 2300 MDT. Law enforcement received a 911 call reporting an airplane crash on a road adjacent to the airport, about 2301 MDT. No witnesses, surveillance video, or flight data captured the accident flight. The airplane's first point of contact (FPOC) was marked by a ground scar about 33 ft inside the airport's eastern perimeter fence near the northeast corner of the airport. Paint chips, the right-wing tip and other debris extended from the FPOC through the perimeter fence to the main wreckage, which came to rest upright on the adjacent road about 30 ft beyond the airport boundary fence. The debris path was oriented about 058° magnetic, and the airplane came to rest on a heading of about 189° magnetic. Crushing and deformation were observed throughout the fuselage, wings, empennage, cockpit, and landing gear. The right wing exhibited leading-edge crushing and compression, with buckling of the upper and lower wing skins. The wing was bent upward near the root, with deformation extending into the midspan section of the wing. Portions of the wing skin were torn and separated. The left wing exhibited extensive buckling of the outboard wing skin and leading edge. The outboard wing was bent upward and aft, with wrinkling extending inboard. The fuselage was crushed, with substantial damage to the cabin and aft fuselage. The vertical stabilizer and rudder exhibited crushing and deformation. The horizontal stabilizer and elevator were bent and partially separated at their attachment points. The two-bladed McCauley propeller was separated from the engine crankshaft and was located within the debris field. Both blades exhibited extensive chordwise scratches along their surfaces. One blade was separated at the blade tip. The other blade exhibited bending near the outboard end, with the blade tip bent aft along with deformation. The propeller spinner was crushed and extensively deformed. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260802203499.s: A Cessna 172G pilot conducting a Part 91 night flight was fatally injured when the aircraft crashed into an airport perimeter fence and adjacent road near Blackfoot, Idaho. The accident caused substantial damage to the airframe and propeller, with no witnesses or data available to determine the specific cause.

NTSB:20260802203501.n: On August 2, 2026, about 1608 central daylight time (CDT), a Beech E18S airplane, N210Q, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Guymon, Oklahoma. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 positioning flight. The airplane was purchased by the pilot on June 22, 2026. According to the seller, the pilot was re-positioning the airplane to South Carolina. The seller stated that he had flown about 6 hours with the pilot in the accident airplane over two flights from June 21 to June 27. The pilot arrived on August 1 to pick up the airplane. The flight took place over multiple time zones, all times referenced will be in CDT. On August 1, the airplane departed Lebanon State Airport (S30), Lebanon, Oregon, about 2108 and arrived at Winnemucca Municipal Airport (WMC), Winnemucca, Nevada, at 0015. The airplane was refueled with 175 gallons of 100 low-lead aviation fuel before departing about 0111, August 2. On August 2, about 0440, the airplane landed at Four Corners Regional Airport (FMN), Farmington, New Mexico. The airplane was refueled with 88 gallons of 100 low-lead aviation. The airplane departed FMN about 1258 for Guymon Municipal Airport (GUY), Guymon, Oklahoma. The airplane landed at GUY about 1509. According to the GUY airport manager, the pilot refueled the airplane with 211.7 gallons of fuel and added oil to both engines. He spoke briefly with the pilot and discussed a fuel stop near Little Rock, Arkansas. At 1606, the pilot announced his departure from runway 18 at GUY on the common traffic advisory frequency (CTAF). According to witnesses, after departing runway 18, the airplane was observed making a left bank and the pilot announced on CTAF that he was departing to the east. Witnesses observed the airplane make a turn to the east and continue the turn to the north while descending in a nose low, left-wing-low attitude. Multiple security videos captured the accident sequence. The footage was sent to the NTSB Vehicle Performance Division for further analysis. The airplane impacted a grass covered field in a wings-level, flat pitch attitude on a heading of about 015°. The aircraft came to rest upright about 80 ft north of the initial impact point. A post-impact fire consumed the majority of the fuselage and melted the wings and tail as seen in figure 1. All major components of the airplane were identified. Both engines were separated from the airframe and located near the main wreckage. Both propeller hubs remained attached to the engines. The propeller blades showed varying degrees of bending, twisting, chordwise scratching and polishing. Examination of the flight controls found no evidence of preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation. Figure 1. Main wreckage The pilot held a commercial certificate with ratings for airplane single-engine land, airplane single-engine sea, airplane multi-engine land, airplane multi-engine sea, instrument airplane and a BE-1900 type rating. Additionally, he held an Airline Transport Pilot certificate for rotorcraft-helicopter. He reported a total flight experience of 12,000 hours on an application for an FAA first-class medical certificate, dated December 24, 2025. The airplane was recovered to a secure facility for further examination.
NTSB:20260802203501.s: A commercial pilot was fatally injured when his Beech E18S crashed near Guymon, Oklahoma, shortly after departing runway 18. Witnesses observed the aircraft descending in a nose-low, left-wing-low attitude before impacting a field and burning, with no pre-impact mechanical failures found.

NTSB:20260803203508.n: On July 30, 2026, at 2356 mountain daylight time, a Cessna 172M airplane, N9650V, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Layton, Utah. The flight instructor was seriously injured, and the private pilot sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title?14 Code of Federal Regulations Part?91 instructional flight. The flight instructor reported that he and the private pilot were conducting a long-distance night cross-country instructional flight. As they were descending to land near the completion of the flight, the engine sputtered and then lost all power. The flight instructor configured the airplane for best-glide performance, declared an emergency with air traffic control, and attempted to restart the engine. The private pilot assisted with checklist items, and both pilots worked together to troubleshoot and restart the engine. Both pilots reported that on about three or four occasions, the engine restarted and ran rough briefly, then lost power. The flight instructor determined the airplane had sufficient altitude and performance to glide to a runway landing at Hill Air Force Base (HIF), which was directly ahead. He reported that a gust of wind from a canyon hit the airplane from the right, resulting in an unexpected altitude loss. The flight instructor then determined the airplane would no longer reach the planned runway and performed a forced landing in a dark area near a roadway south of the airport. The airplane landed hard, nosed over and came to rest inverted in an intersection, sustaining substantial damage to the wings and fuselage. A mobile phone video, recorded by a resident who lives near the accident location, showed the airplane descending low over a residential neighborhood. In the video, the engine produced a popping sound and was running sporadically. A witness who was driving her vehicle on the roadway near the accident intersection reported that she observed something passing above. The witness then heard a loud crashing sound and observed an airplane overturned alongside the intersection. She noted that she did not hear sound coming from the airplane prior to the accident. First responders reported seeing fuel pouring from the airplane wreckage, which continued to leak from the left wing for up to two hours after the crash. The wreckage was transported to a secure facility and retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260803203508.s: During a night instructional flight in a Cessna 172M, the engine lost power while descending to land, causing the flight instructor and private pilot to attempt a forced landing. A gust of wind from a canyon caused unexpected altitude loss, resulting in a hard landing where the aircraft nosed over, inverted, and sustained substantial damage.

NTSB:20260803203509.n: The pilot of the tailwheel equipped airplane reported that he conducted a preflight inspection of the airplane, departed from the airport, and remained in the traffic pattern. While on final approach to land, the airplane landed prior to the runway threshold. The main landing gear contacted the edge of the runway pavement, which protruded out about 12 inches above the surface, resulting in damage to the right landing gear. The airplane pitched nose down, impacted the runway surface, then overturned and came to rest inverted. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the right wing lift strut. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260803203509.s: The pilot of a tailwheel airplane landed short of the runway threshold on final approach, striking a 12-inch pavement edge with the right main gear. This impact caused the aircraft to pitch nose down, overturn, and sustain substantial damage to the right wing lift strut, with no preaccident mechanical failures reported.

NTSB:20260804203515.n: The pilot was making a right pedal turn in an attempt to land on the helipad when the tail rotor struck a standpipe on the fuel farm. The helicopter began to become unstable, but the pilot immediately lowered the collective and the helicopter landed upright on the helipad. Neither the pilot nor the two crew members were injured. Postaccident examination of the helicopter revealed damage to the tail rotor blades and substantial damage to the tail rotor gear box. The operator reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures of the helicopter that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260804203515.s: During a right pedal turn for landing, the helicopter's tail rotor struck a fuel farm standpipe, causing instability. The pilot lowered the collective to land upright with no injuries, though the tail rotor blades and gearbox sustained substantial damage.

NTSB:20260804203517.n: On August 2, 2026, about 1318 central daylight time, a Robinson Helicopter Company R44 II helicopter, N26KL, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Bennett, Iowa. The pilot was not injured. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 137 agricultural flight. The pilot reported that as the helicopter passed over a tree line he felt a vibration in the airframe and when the vibration increased he decided to perform an autorotation into the next field. According to the pilot, the helicopter descended rapidly from about 20 ft above the ground which resulted in a hard landing. A witness to the accident reported hearing an "awful" noise before the helicopter passed over a tree. The witness stated that as the helicopter descended the main rotor blades almost stopped rotating when the helicopter was about 10 to 15 ft above the ground, and then the helicopter dropped vertically into the field. The airframe and tailboom sustained substantial damage during the hard landing. The helicopter was recovered to a secure facility pending an examination.
NTSB:20260804203517.s: During a Part 137 agricultural flight, the pilot of a Robinson R44 II helicopter reported airframe vibration and performed an autorotation after passing a tree line. The helicopter descended rapidly from about 20 feet, resulting in a hard landing and substantial damage to the airframe and tailboom.

NTSB:20260804203519.n: On August 2, 2026, about 1223 central daylight time, a Taylorcraft BC12-D airplane, N43665 was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Boyceville, Wisconsin. Both the pilot and passenger were seriously injured. The airplane was operated under Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 as a personal flight. According to the passenger, they departed from Marshfield, Wisconsin, earlier in the day and then flew to Red Wing, Minnesota, and then Boyceville, Wisconsin. He said that the engine performed normally and neither he nor the pilot were concerned about the airplane's performance. The passenger said that before they left Boyceville, the pilot performed a preflight check, which included checking the oil and fuel levels. Shortly after the airplane departed from Boyceville, about 75 to 100 ft above the ground, the engine began to sputter and cut in and out. The passenger stated that the pilot maneuvered the airplane away from trees and then the engine quite completely. The airplane impacted a cornfield. The fuselage and both wings were substantially damaged. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260804203519.s: A pilot and passenger were seriously injured when their Taylorcraft BC12-D suffered an engine failure shortly after departing Boyceville, Wisconsin. The engine sputtered and quit at 75 to 100 feet, causing the aircraft to impact a cornfield with substantial damage to the fuselage and wings.

NTSB:20260804203521.n: The flight instructor reported that at some point between the base turn and final approach, the landing gear selector switch was inadvertently moved to the UP or gear retracted position. Unknown to the flight instructor or the pilot receiving instruction, the airplane subsequently landed with the landing gear retracted and sustained substantial damage to the lower fuselage. Postaccident examination of the landing gear selector switch revealed that the safety notch was worn and allowed the switch to move from the DOWN position to the UP position with minimal force. The worn condition of the safety notch could have increased the likelihood of an inadvertent movement of the selector switch during flight.
NTSB:20260804203521.s: A flight instructor and student landed an airplane with the gear retracted between the base turn and final approach, causing substantial fuselage damage. The accident resulted from a worn safety notch on the landing gear selector switch that allowed inadvertent movement to the UP position.

NTSB:20260805203525.n: On August 4, 2026, about 1839 central daylight time, a Piper PA-24-250 airplane, N8422P, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Bethany, Missouri. The pilot received fatal injuries. The airplane was operated under Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations as a Part 91 flight. The pilot, who was also the airplane owner, departed on a personal flight under visual flight rules from Peoria International Airport Peoria, Illinois, to Rapid City Regional Airport, Rapid City, South Dakota. Preliminary radar data showed that the flight climbed to an initial cruise altitude of about 13,000 ft msl after departure and operated at an altitude about 12,500 ft msl for about 90 minutes. The cruise altitude increased above 18,000 ft msl and into Class A airspace during the flight, which operated without air traffic control clearance or services. A review of weather data showed the flight entered convective activity after which it descended and impacted terrain. The airplane was destroyed by impact forces and a postcrash fire. Postaccident examination of the airplane revealed that it was not equipped with an installed breathable or a portable breathable oxygen system. The postaccident examination revealed no mechanical anomalies that would have precluded normal airplane operation.
NTSB:20260805203525.s: The pilot of a Piper PA-24-250 entered Class A airspace above 18,000 feet without clearance or an oxygen system. The aircraft impacted terrain after entering convective activity, destroying the airplane and killing the pilot.

NTSB:20260805203526.n: On August 4, 2026, at about 1845 Pacific daylight time, a Cirrus Design Corporation SR22T airplane, N625LK, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Bend, Oregon. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to preliminary ADS-B data, the airplane departed from runway 35 at Bend Municipal Airport (BDN), Bend, Oregon, at about 1335. The airplane flew westbound, climbing to about 11,000 ft mean sea level (msl), before executing multiple turns above mountainous terrain about 33 miles west of BDN. Between about 1415 and 1610, the airplane maintained a looping, meandering flight path in the vicinity of BDN. At about 1610, the airplane began to fly in circles at about 5,000 ft msl 12 miles west of BDN. The final ten seconds of data captured by the airplane's recoverable data module (RDM) showed that the airplane's left fuel tank sensor indicated 0 gallons of fuel remaining and the right fuel tank sensor indicated 1 gallon of fuel remaining. The RDM data also indicated that the airplane's pitch moved from about 4° nose down to about 22° nose down and the throttle lever angle was at 92.3%. The RDM data terminated at 1845:50. The airplane impacted terrain 12.5 miles west of BDN. The area was generally flat, with short scrub brush and standing dead trees. The first identified points of impact consisted of an area of fallen dead trees and a shallow impact crater. The wreckage path was about 175 ft long, oriented on a magnetic heading of 092°. The left wing, left aileron, right elevator, two propeller blades, left cabin door, fiberglass fragments, and fragments of the windscreen were distributed throughout the wreckage path. The main wreckage came to rest inverted on a magnetic heading of 333°. The airplane was recovered for further examination.
NTSB:20260805203526.s: A pilot operating a Cirrus SR22T under Part 91 was fatally injured when the aircraft impacted terrain near Bend, Oregon. Preliminary data indicated the accident occurred after the left fuel tank sensor read zero gallons and the right tank read one gallon, resulting in a nose-down pitch and loss of control.
