NTSB:20260805203529.s: Marine One (VM1) and Envoy Air flight 3742 (ENY3742) experienced a loss of separation near DCA due to failed radio communications preventing the required 3-minute departure call. The aircraft passed within 0.82 miles laterally and 700 feet vertically, but both flights completed their missions without injury.

NTSB:20260805203531.n: The pilot stated that he had performed a preflight inspection of the airplane and did not note any deficiency with the engine cowling's security. About 7 minutes into the flight, the front right engine cowling opened and started flapping. The pilot declared an emergency with air traffic control and diverted to a nearby airport where he landed uneventfully. Postaccident examination of the airplane revealed that engine baffling had separated from the engine compartment and impacted the right elevator resulting in substantial damage. Maintenance personnel examined the airplane after the accident and found that the cowling's latch mechanism functioned normally with no mechanical irregularities.
NTSB:20260805203531.s: The pilot reported that seven minutes into flight, the right engine cowling opened and flapped, causing an emergency diversion and uneventful landing. Post-accident examination found separated engine baffling damaged the right elevator, though the cowling latch mechanism functioned normally.

NTSB:20260806203539.n: On August 6, 2026, about 1030 central daylight time, a Beech H35, N5409D, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Bogalusa, Louisiana. The private pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. Preliminary ADS-B data showed the airplane departed Elm Creek Airpark (0TX6), Seguin, Texas, where the airplane was based, at 0617. The airplane arrived at George R Carr Memorial Air Field (BXA), Bogalusa, Louisiana, about 0915. According to the airport manager at BXA, the pilot wanted 40 gallons of fuel. He continued that the pilot “topped off” the left and right main fuel tanks and was adding fuel to the right auxiliary fuel tank when the fuel farm pump motor stopped working. The pilot had added 35 gallons at that point and told the airport manager that this would be enough fuel. The airport manager also reported that the pilot had wanted to put more fuel into the right side of the airplane to help “get the plane trimmed better.” The airport manager asked the pilot if he planned to use the crew vehicle to go into town to get something to eat, the pilot told him no, that they had left early and were on their way to Florida. Motion-activated surveillance cameras at the airport showed the pilot and passenger in the fixed base operator (FBO) building and the airport manager reported that he spoke with the pilot about the next leg of their flight to Florida. The pilot told him that they would stop on their way back to Texas the following Tuesday. The airport manager then left to begin working on the fuel farm pump and the cameras show the pilot and passenger leaving the FBO at 1013. The cameras that were pointed at the ramp did not capture any other footage of the pilot and passenger, or the accident airplane. The airport manager continued that while at the fuel farm working on the pump he saw the pilot doing a walkaround but did not watch the full preflight inspection and was not sure if the pilot sumped the airplane’s fuel tanks. He then heard the pilot start the engine, which took two tries before it started. He watched as the airplane taxied out to the runway and heard the pilot perform an engine run-up. He then watched the takeoff roll, rotation, and initial climb before he turned and began putting tools away. When he exited the fuel farm pit and began to place his tools in his truck, he saw a smoke plume and went to the accident site where he found the airplane consumed by a postimpact fire. He did not report hearing any abnormalities in the engine noise during the engine run-up or takeoff/initial climb. The accident site was located about 0.5 statute miles from the departure end of runway 36, the runway the airplane departed from, in a forested area. A pine tree about 10 ft aft and outboard of the right wing tip had two branches broken about 40 ft up the tree with the higher branch broken closer to the trunk. A large log was embedded in the cowling and cabin compartment of the wreckage, and a broken stump was observed under the fuselage consistent with the diameter of the embedded log. Multiple pieces of wood were observed with clean 45° angle cuts and the ends were singed. The wreckage came to rest on a true heading of about 300°, at an elevation of 148 ft mean sea level (msl). All major components of the airplane were located with the main wreckage. The wreckage debris field was contained to about a 15 yard radius encompassing the main wreckage. Postaccident fire damage was observed for about a 50 yard radius around the accident site. The fuselage was mostly consumed by postimpact fire. The main cabin door was observed in the main wreckage and was substantially damaged by fire. The baggage door and emergency escape hatch were consumed by fire and not observed. The empennage was thermally damaged and remained attached to the fuselage via the control cables. Both stabilizers remained attached to the empennage. Both ruddervators remained attached to the stabilizers and the trim tabs remained attached to the ruddervators. Both wing leading edges were impact crushed aft to the forward spar and the upper and lower wing skin, aft of the forward wing spar, was wrinkled. The right wing impacted a tree, about 5 inches in diameter, about 5 ft from the base and slid down the tree removing bark until the wing came to rest on the ground. Both flaps and ailerons remained attached to their respective wings. The left flap actuator was measured, based on this measurement the flaps were at or near the “UP” position. The right flap actuator was consumed by fire and was unable to be measured. The landing gear actuator housing, motor, and landing gear extension handle were consumed by fire. The sector gear and main landing gear pushrods remained, and the position of the pushrods corresponded to the landing gear being fully extended or nearly so, if in an intermediate position. The faceplate for the tachometer was recovered with the needle fixed at a high rpm; due to thermal damage the exact reading could not be determined. All fuel tanks were destroyed by postaccident fire. When low pressure air was blown through the fuel selector it was found to be in the AUX position. The fuel strainer screen was examined and was unobstructed. The strainer bowl was examined and did not contain any debris or signs of corrosion. The impact crater created by the engine was about 18 inches in depth. The engine exhibited impact and fire damage. Multiple accessories were impact separated from the engine. The throttle, mixture, and propeller controls were impact-separated. The airplane was equipped with one standard and one electronic magneto; both magnetos were impact-separated. The oil pan was destroyed by impact forces. The oil filter remained attached to the oil filter adapter and was not removed. The oil filler cap and dipstick remained installed in their respective locations. The propeller remained attached to the engine crankshaft flange. Both propeller blades remained installed and attached to the propeller hub. The propeller governor remained attached to the engine and the governor actuator rod arm was impact separated. One propeller blade was curved slightly aft. The other blade exhibited significant S bending and twisting. The spinner was crushed around the propeller dome. The airplane was recovered and retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260806203539.s: A private pilot and passenger were fatally injured when their Beech H35 crashed shortly after takeoff from Bogalusa, Louisiana, while operating under Part 91. The aircraft struck trees and caught fire, with the fuel selector found in the AUX position and no pre-accident engine abnormalities reported by witnesses.

NTSB:20260806203540.n: On August 5, 2026, at 1117 mountain daylight time, a Cessna 177B, N34852, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Perris, California. The flight instructor and student pilot were not injured. The airplane was being operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight. According to both pilots, after completing a series of maneuvers, the engine lost power while positioning the airplane to practice S-turns at 1,500 ft AGL. Attempts to restart the engine were unsuccessful so the flight instructor performed an emergency landing to a field. During landing the airplane struck vegetation and nosed over, resulting in substantial damage to the left wing and fuselage. The pilots reported 44 gallons of fuel onboard at takeoff and they had been airborne about 1.5 hrs when the engine quit.
NTSB:20260806203540.s: A flight instructor and student pilot in a Cessna 177B experienced total engine power loss at 1,500 ft AGL during S-turn practice. The instructor executed an emergency field landing where the aircraft struck vegetation and nosed over, causing substantial damage to the left wing and fuselage.

NTSB:20260807203543.n: The pilot reported that while completing his preflight checks of the airplane, he thought that he had closed and locked its canopy, though he did not push up after locking it as was his usual habit. Shortly after starting the takeoff roll for a local flight, the canopy opened and struck the airplane's right wing, substantially damaging the canopy. The pilot immediately aborted the takeoff and taxied back to the ramp without further incident. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260807203543.s: The pilot reported that during the takeoff roll of a local flight, the canopy opened and struck the right wing because he failed to push it up after locking. He aborted the takeoff and taxied back to the ramp with substantial canopy damage but no mechanical failures.

NTSB:20260807203544.n: The pilot stated while on final approach to land, he was facing directly into the sun. The airplane touched down about 1,000 ft from the runway threshold, and during the landing roll the pilot spotted a deer running across the runway from left to right. He immediately added full power and set approach flaps to abort the landing. The pilot then heard a "thud" and the airplane yawed to the left. He immediately reduced engine power and landed the airplane on the remaining runway. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the empennage the left flap as a result of the collision with the deer. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260807203544.s: During final approach, the pilot aborted a landing after spotting a deer on the runway, but the aircraft struck the animal, causing a left yaw and substantial damage to the empennage and left flap. The pilot completed the landing on the remaining runway with no pre-accident mechanical failures reported.

NTSB:20260807203546.n: On August 7, 2026, about 1044 mountain daylight time, a Helicopter Transport Services (Sikorsky) CH-54A Skycrane Helitanker, N793HT, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Cove Fort, Utah. The pilot and copilot were fatally injured. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 133 aerial firefighting flight. The helicopter, owned and operated by Helicopter Transport Services, was conducting aerial fire suppression operations under an exclusive-use contract with the United States Forest Service (USFS) in support of the Wide Mouth 2 Fire in central Utah. It was equipped with a 2,650-gallon water tank and a retractable hover-snorkel system. According to the USFS, the helicopter departed Richfield Municipal Airport (RIF) about 1021 and proceeded toward the Wide Mouth 2 Fire to begin firefighting operations. After departure, the flight crew established radio communications with the aerial supervisor and received authorization to enter the temporary flight restriction (TFR) area surrounding the fire. The aerial supervisor briefed the crew on the initial firefighting objectives, which included coordinated aerial water-drop operations. The helicopter proceeded to a predetermined water source, filled its tank, and then continued to the designated drop area as directed. As the helicopter approached the drop site, the aerial supervisor transferred communications to the ground supervisor, who provided specific instructions regarding the target area. According to the ground supervisor, the helicopter arrived from the northwest, and he directed the crew to the location where water was needed. The helicopter then flew over the area to verify the target, and the flight crew confirmed they had identified the correct location. The crew subsequently reported that they would make another pass before releasing the water load. While maneuvering in a right turn, the helicopter disappeared behind a knoll. The ground supervisor then heard a radio transmission stating, “Oh (expletive), we have a problem,” followed about one second later by, “Mayday, mayday, mayday.” No further communications were received from the helicopter. The helicopter impacted rising terrain, and a post-crash fire consumed much of the airframe (see figure 1). Figure 1. Aerial overview of accident site. (U.S. Forest Service Drone Photo) The investigator-in-charge from the NTSB’s Alaska Regional Office, accompanied by an NTSB aerospace engineer and helicopter specialist, responded to the accident site and examined the wreckage on August 9, 2026. During the on-scene investigation, components were retained for further examination and testing. The results of those examinations are pending. Recovery of the wreckage will take place when fire conditions and logistical considerations allow. A detailed examination of the airframe and engines is pending.
NTSB:20260807203546.s: Helicopter Transport Services pilots flying a Sikorsky CH-54A Skycrane on an aerial firefighting mission near Cove Fort, Utah, were fatally injured when the helicopter impacted rising terrain. The crash occurred during a right turn maneuver behind a knoll while the crew was verifying a water drop target.

NTSB:20260808203552.n: On August 7, 2026, about 1549 mountain daylight time, a Textron Aviation Inc. 172S, N1842E, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Provo, Utah. The flight instructor sustained serious injuries, and the pilot undergoing instruction was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight. The flight was operated by ATP Flight School under the callsign Career Track (CXK) 138 and was intended to provide preparation for the pilot undergoing instruction’s upcoming instrument checkride. The airplane was scheduled to depart for the practice area south of the airport via the “Golf Course” departure, a route that would have initially taken the airplane east over Provo Bay. Preliminary air traffic control audio indicated that multiple aircraft operating in the vicinity of Provo Municipal Airport (PVU) in the period before the accident reported moderate to severe turbulence. One of those airplanes, which was also operated by ATP, reported descent rates exceeding 1,000 ft per minute while approaching Bird Island, a reporting point in Utah Lake about 5 miles southwest of the airport. At about 1546, the accident airplane was cleared for takeoff from runway 18. ADS-B data showed that the airplane began a climbing left turn to the southeast with a groundspeed that varied between 68 and 75 knots. A few seconds later, the airplane began a rapid descent, accelerating to a groundspeed of about 96 knots before the last ADS-B target was recorded approximately 160 ft above the water, and 350 ft short of the accident site. Figure 1 – ADS-B track Security camera footage from multiple buildings located on the east side of the airport, facing west and south-southwest, showed several areas of tall dust formations moving through the surface area along and south of the airport during the time preceding the accident. One dust formation appeared to move across the departure end of runway 18 as the airplane entered the video frame in the upper-right portion of one of the cameras. A few seconds later, the airplane began to descend, and a splash was observed about 30 seconds later as the airplane impacted the water. The airplane came to rest in marshland within Provo Bay, about 6,000 ft south-southeast of the departure end of runway 18. The main wreckage was semi-submerged in about 18 inches of water and resting on soft mud. The debris field extended about 100 ft in length. The first identified point of impact was the nose landing gear assembly, which had separated from the airframe. The remaining wreckage was concentrated to the east of that location. The forward cabin section, engine, and both wings were submerged, with a section of a propeller blade tip visible above the water. The wreckage was recovered for further examination.
NTSB:20260808203552.s: An ATP Flight School Cessna 172S instructor and student were fatally injured when the aircraft crashed into Provo Bay shortly after takeoff from Runway 18. The accident occurred during an instrument training flight amid reported severe turbulence and observed dust formations, causing a rapid descent and impact with the water.

NTSB:20260810203553.n: On August 9, 2026, at about 1655 central daylight time, an experimental amateur-built Avid Mark IV, N77FB, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Arp, Texas. The private pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to witnesses, the accident airplane and a second airplane had landed in a grass field earlier in the afternoon. The accident airplane subsequently departed the field first and remained in the vicinity while the second airplane departed. Witnesses reported that after takeoff, the accident airplane was flying at a low altitude and appeared to be moving slowly as it maneuvered near the second airplane. The accident airplane then entered a steep left bank, followed by a steep descending turn. The airplane subsequently impacted trees and terrain adjacent to the field. The airplane came to rest with all major components located at the accident site. The fuselage sustained impact damage, and both wings remained attached to the fuselage. Examination of the airframe confirmed flight control continuity, and no evidence of preimpact flight control anomaly was observed. Both wing fuel tanks remained intact and contained fuel. Examination of the engine confirmed mechanical continuity and compression on all cylinders. No evidence of a preimpact mechanical anomaly was observed that would have precluded normal operation. An electronic flight instrument was recovered and retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260810203553.s: A private pilot flying an experimental Avid Mark IV was fatally injured when the aircraft impacted trees and terrain near Arp, Texas, during a low-altitude maneuver. The pilot entered a steep left bank and descending turn after takeoff, with no preimpact mechanical or flight control anomalies found.

NTSB:20260810203555.n: On August 9, 2026 at 802 eastern daylight time, a Mooney M20E, N9257V, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Conway, South Carolina. The pilot was uninjured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported he planned to conduct an instrument flight rules (IFR) cross-country flight from Conway-Horry County Airport (HYW), Conway, South Carolina, to Berkeley County Airport (MKS), Moncks Corner, South Carolina. The pilot stated that he performed an engine run-up, which included a check of the magnetos, propeller governor and auxiliary fuel pump. He then departed runway 22, announced his intention to depart the area on the common traffic advisory frequency and switched to the terminal radar approach control frequency to activate his IFR clearance. Shortly thereafter, he noticed “sluggish” performance and decided to switch fuel tanks, which did not resolve the condition. He soon felt a vibration and noticed the engine running rough, which he described as continuing to “pick up and then back off.” About 1,000 ft mean sea level, he turned back to HYW before the engine lost power completely. The pilot stated that he could not reach the airport and soon began striking trees. The airplane came to rest upright, in dense woods. Post accident examination of the airplane by an FAA inspector revealed substantial damage to the empennage, fuselage, and both wings. The fuselage was crumpled and torn in multiple locations, and both the wings and tail sustained significant leading-edge damage. The engine case was not breached, and the engine oil dipstick was removed and showed about 8 quarts of oil. The pilot stated that he refueled the airplane after his last flight in June 2026 to a total of 52 gallons. The most recent maintenance logbook entry noted the replacement of the engine starter in July 2026. The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260810203555.s: The pilot of a Mooney M20E experienced engine roughness and power loss shortly after departing Conway-Horry County Airport for an IFR flight. Unable to return to the airport, the aircraft struck trees and sustained substantial damage, though the pilot remained uninjured.

NTSB:20260810203557.n: On August 6, 2026, about 1538 central daylight time, a PZL-Bielsko B1-PW-5 glider, N105WS, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Briggs, Texas. The pilot was fatally injured. The glider was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The glider was departing on an auto-tow launch at the time of the accident. According to witness statements, the glider achieved level flight at about 1,000 ft before release from the towline. Following the release, the glider yawed to the right and entered a descending spiral, completing about 7 to 8 rotations before impacting terrain west of the glider port. Witnesses reported that the glider impacted the ground in a near-vertical attitude. The cockpit and forward fuselage were crushed aft during the impact. Both wings remained attached to the fuselage. The tail section and vertical stabilizer were partially separated, with the aft 4 ft of the tail boom folded over the aft fuselage. The glider was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260810203557.s: A pilot was fatally injured when a PZL-Bielsko B1-PW-5 glider, N105WS, was substantially damaged during an auto-tow launch near Briggs, Texas. After release at 1,000 ft, the glider yawed right, entered a descending spiral, and impacted terrain in a near-vertical attitude.

NTSB:20260810203559.n: The pilot stated that he had just landed on the runway and was instructed by the tower controller to exit the runway to the left and taxi to the hangars. After exiting the runway, he stopped past the hold short line to perform the after-landing checklist. While he was performing the checklist items, the airplane was struck from behind by a fuel truck, resulting in substantial damage to the airplane's empennage, elevators, and fuselage. The fuel truck driver stated that he was looking at his phone while he was crossing the runway and when he looked up, he saw the airplane in front of him. He applied the truck's brakes, but the truck struck the airplane.
NTSB:20260810203559.s: After landing and exiting the runway, a pilot stopped past the hold short line for the after-landing checklist when a fuel truck struck the aircraft's empennage. The truck driver reported looking at his phone while crossing the runway, causing him to miss the airplane until it was too late to stop.

NTSB:20260810203560.n: On August 6, 2026, about 1355 eastern daylight time, a Piper Aircraft PA-32-260 airplane, N8791E, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Pinetown, North Carolina. The private pilot and two passengers sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the pilot, after departing Martin County Airport (MCZ), Williamston, North Carolina, enroute to Ocracoke Island Airport (W95), Ocracoke, North Carolina, he climbed to and leveled at 3,000 ft mean sea level. About 10 minutes after establishing cruise flight, the engine experienced a total loss of power. The pilot established the airplane's best-glide airspeed, transmitted a mayday call, and attempted to restart the engine. Unable to restore engine power, he selected a logging path within a wooded area for a forced landing. During the landing rollout, the airplane's left wing struck a tree. The airplane subsequently impacted another tree and came to rest in a ditch, resulting in substantial damage to the wings and fuselage. The wreckage was recovered to a secure facility for further examination.
NTSB:20260810203560.s: A private pilot flying a Piper PA-32-260 from Martin County to Ocracoke Island experienced a total engine power loss at 3,000 feet. The pilot attempted a forced landing in a wooded area, but the left wing struck a tree, causing substantial damage to the aircraft and minor injuries to the occupants.

NTSB:20260810203562.n: On August 10, 2026, about 1248 central daylight time, an experimental Velocity 173 FG Elite II airplane, N6954K, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Palmyra, Illinois. The pilot and two passengers sustained no injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal cross-country flight. According to the pilot, 14 gallons of 100 low lead fuel was purchased prior to the flight at the St. Louis Regional Airport (ALN), East Alton, Illinois. The airplane departed from ALN about 1210, and the destination was the Whiteside County Airport (SQI), Rock Falls, Illinois, where the pilot based the airplane. The airplane climbed to about 7,500 ft msl and established a cruise flight configuration. About 15 minutes later, the engine sustained a total loss of power. The pilot declared an emergency with air traffic control. The pilot coordinated with the controller, and he decided to divert to the nearest airport, the Zelmer Memorial Airpark (5K1), Palmyra, Illinois. During the emergency descent, he attempted to restore the engine power. He noticed that partial engine power was restored by pulling the mixture control nearly to the idle cutoff position. He further noticed that further attempts at a richer setting caused a loss of engine power. The pilot maneuvered the airplane for a straight-in approach to runway 18 at 5K1. He noted that the approach was too high and too fast. During the landing, the airplane departed the runway to the left. The airplane came to rest upright in a flat soybean field. The experimental canard airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage, the right wing, and the right canard. Postaccident examination found the fuel system to be intact, and the two wing fuel tanks were found to be more than half full. A fuel sample did not reveal any contamination. According to the pilot, there is no fuel selector valve assembly installed, only a fuel cutoff control. The two wing fuel tanks feed into a single header fuel tank. The airplane was recovered from the accident site, and it was transported to a secure location for future examination. The composite airplane was built from a kit in 1998. A review of FAA records showed that the pilot purchased the airplane in May 2008. The airplane was equipped with a Lycoming Engines IO-360-C1D6 reciprocating engine and a MT-Propeller MTV-18-B/LD168-101 controllable pitch three blade wood-composite propeller. A review of the airplane’s maintenance records showed that a condition inspection was performed by a mechanic on February 15, 2026, for the airframe, the engine, and the propeller. The airplane accumulated 23.7 hours since the condition inspection.
NTSB:20260810203562.s: The pilot of an experimental Velocity 173 experienced total engine power loss at 7,500 feet, likely due to improper mixture control settings, and diverted to Zelmer Memorial Airpark. The aircraft departed the runway during landing and sustained substantial damage to the fuselage, right wing, and canard, though all occupants were uninjured.

NTSB:20260811203563.n: On August 5, 2026, at about 1034 mountain daylight time, a Van's Aircraft RV-8, C-GFWR, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Great Falls, Montana. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The airplane departed Villeneuve Airport (CZVL), near Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, and landed on runway 21 at Great Falls International Airport (KGTF), Great Falls, Montana. During the landing rollout, the airplane veered right. The pilot applied engine power while attempting to regain directional control, and the airplane subsequently ground looped to the right and departed the runway. The left main landing gear collapsed, and the left wing contacted the ground. The airplane came to rest in the grass adjacent to the runway. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the left wing, and fuselage. The pilot reported that the tailwheel assembly had been replaced about two weeks before the accident and that the accident flight was the airplane's first flight and landing since the replacement. The airplane was retained for examination.
NTSB:20260811203563.s: The pilot of a Van's RV-8, C-GFWR, ground looped right during landing rollout at Great Falls International Airport after applying power to correct a veer. The accident, occurring on the first flight since a tailwheel replacement, caused left main gear collapse and substantial damage to the wing and fuselage.

NTSB:20260811203564.n: On August 10, 2026, about 12:55 Pacific daylight time, a Cessna 180, N180DT, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near La Center, Washington. The flight instructor and pilot receiving instruction were seriously injured. The flight was being operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight. According to preliminary ADS-B, the airplane departed from runway 31 at Daybreak (WA46), La Center, Washington, about 1250, turned to the northwest, and climbed to 1,025 ft above ground level (agl). At 1251, the airplane made a turn to the east, and continued its climb to 2,200 ft. As the airplane passed the departure end of runway 31, it began a descent and about .5 mile east-southeast of WA46, the airplane made a left turn to the north. 1 mile northeast of WA46, at about 1,200 ft agl, the airplane made a descending 180° turn to the left, and flew southbound, approximately parallel with runway 13/31 at WA46, and about .45 mile from runway 13/31. About .40 mile east of the approach end of runway 31, about 250 ft agl, the airplane began a right turn and continued its descent until the end of the available flight track data. The last recorded data point was at 1255, about .23 mile southeast of the approach end of runway 31. (See figure 1) Figure 1. Preliminary ADS-B flight track data of accident flight. According to a witness who was positioned to the east of WA46, he observed the airplane shortly before the accident. He observed the airplane as it made the northbound turn, east of WA46, and then again as it flew southbound and began its turn toward the runway. He stated that as it was approaching, the engine sounded like it “backfired, as if the pilot was throttling back for landing”, and that otherwise, the airplane looked and sounded like most other airplanes he observes. According to a family friend, the flight instructor stated to him that “they had been doing some practicing at Daybreak and that the engine lost power, they came up short and they had to put it in the trees.” The friend stated that the pilot had disclosed additional detail to him but did not share it with NTSB. Due to ongoing medical circumstances at the time of this report, the NTSB has not received a statement of events from either pilot. The airplane came to rest inverted, about 380 ft southeast of WA46. Postaccident examination of the airplane revealed substantial damage to both wings, the vertical stabilizer, and the fuselage. The wreckage was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260811203564.s: A flight instructor and student in a Cessna 180 were seriously injured when the aircraft crashed near La Center, Washington, during a Part 91 instructional flight. The instructor reported that the engine lost power, causing the airplane to come up short and impact the trees.

NTSB:20260811203571.n: On August 10, 2026, at about 1835 mountain daylight time, an experimental amateur built Glasair Sportsman 2 Plus 2 airplane, N202AZ, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Pine, Arizona. The pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to preliminary ADS-B data, the airplane departed from runway 06 at Payson Airport (PAN), Payson, Arizona about 1827:07. The airplane flew on a northwest heading, climbing to about 5,850 ft mean sea level (msl) at 1831:51, before turning to the southwest above mountainous terrain about 7 nautical miles (nm) northwest of PAN. The airplane proceeded to the southwest and descended into a canyon, when the ADS-B signal was lost at 1835:47, about an altitude of 4,675 ft msl (about 680 ft above ground level and 136 ft above the canyon rim). The airplane impacted terrain about 3 nm west of the last ADS-B data point, on the northwestern face of a draw at an elevation of about 3,994 ft msl. The accident site area was comprised of roughly 45° sloping terrain with desert junipers and prickly pear cacti scattered along the rocky slope. The first identifiable point of impact (FIPOI) was a desert juniper with separated and damaged branches along with the left wing tip located at the base of the tree. The FIPOI was located about 791 ft above the base of the ravine, and about 1,300 ft below the ridgeline. The wreckage debris path was about 102 ft in length and oriented on a magnetic heading of 175°. The left wing, left aileron, left flap, right wing tip, fuselage, empennage, and engine were distributed throughout the wreckage debris path. A majority of the wreckage was consumed by a post impact fire. The fuselage came to rest in a right wing low, nose down attitude, on a heading of about 022 ° magnetic. The propeller was separated from the crankshaft aft of the propeller flange. Both propeller blades exhibited “S” bending, and leading-edge gouges. The wreckage was recovered to a secure location for further examination.
NTSB:20260811203571.s: The pilot and passenger of an experimental Glasair Sportsman 2 Plus 2 were fatally injured when the aircraft impacted terrain near Pine, Arizona, during a Part 91 personal flight. The airplane descended into a canyon and struck a sloping draw after turning southwest above mountainous terrain, resulting in a post-impact fire that consumed most of the wreckage.

NTSB:20260811203572.n: On August 9, 2026, at 1420 mountain daylight time, a Cessna 208B airplane, N247JP, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Salmon, Idaho. The pilot and eight passengers were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 135 on-demand air taxi flight. The pilot reported that, after an uneventful flight from the departure airport, he joined the downwind leg of the traffic pattern for runway 17. While turning onto the base leg, he extended the wing flaps in preparation for landing and subsequently heard a loud "pop." Immediately thereafter, the airplane made an aggressive, uncommanded roll to the left and banked to about 45°. The pilot attempted to regain lateral control by applying right aileron. He moved the control yoke to the full right aileron position and adjusted the aileron trim to the full right setting. The airplane touched down normally, and the pilot taxied it to the ramp without further incident. Following the landing, a company mechanic examined the flight control systems and found substantial damage to the left wing spar. A preliminary examination identified a loose flap bolt that allowed the lower portion of the aft bellcrank to move freely. The aft bellcrank was designed to attach to the airplane with a bolt secured to an anchor nut assembly on its lower surface (see figure 1). The hardware will be retained for further examination. Figure 1: Diagram showing the location of the loose bolt
NTSB:20260811203572.s: The pilot of a Cessna 208B Part 135 air taxi experienced an uncommanded 45° left roll during the base leg after a loud pop caused by a loose flap bolt. This hardware failure allowed the aft bellcrank to move freely, damaging the left wing spar, though the pilot landed safely with no injuries.

NTSB:20260811203576.n: On July 25, 2026, about 1630 central daylight time, a Cessna 150M, N18YZ, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Ferris, Texas. One pilot sustained minor injuries and the other pilot had no injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. Both pilots reported no abnormalities during the preflight. They added a quart of oil to the engine which was at 3.25 quarts when they checked. They fueled the airplane and taxied to the run-up area where the airplane showed normal indications during the preflight operational checks. The airplane departed from runway 13 at the Lancaster Regional Airport (LNC), Lancaster, Texas. During the initial climb the right seat pilot at the controls observed a climb rate of about 200 feet per minute and recognized the airplane was not producing sufficient performance to safely continue the flight. About 900 ft msl, the pilots agreed that clearing the power lines and trees ahead of them before initiating a turn was their priority. The engine was producing enough power to maintain airplane altitude but the airplane could not climb. After the airplane cleared the power lines and a residential area, the right seat pilot transferred control of the airplane to the left seat pilot and a turn back to the airport was initiated. As the airplane headed toward the runway, the engine began to run rough and the engine RPM decreased. About 3 miles from the airport the engine lost all power. Without enough altitude to glide to runway 31 an emergency landing was performed which resulted in substantial damage to the engine mount structure. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260811203576.s: Two pilots operating a Cessna 150M experienced low climb performance and subsequent engine power loss during initial climb from Lancaster Regional Airport. The resulting emergency landing caused substantial damage to the engine mount structure after the aircraft cleared obstacles but lacked altitude to return to the runway.

NTSB:20260812203578.n: The flight crew reported that, while in the traffic pattern and turning from base to final, a large bird impacted the leading edge of the left wing, which resulted?in substantial damage to the wing structure. The pilot was able to land safely on the intended runway. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260812203578.s: The flight crew reported a large bird strike on the left wing leading edge while turning from base to final, causing substantial structural damage. The pilot landed safely on the intended runway and confirmed no pre-accident mechanical malfunctions.

NTSB:20260813203582.n: On August 12, 2026, about 1906 eastern daylight time, a Staudacher ZZ 102 experimental airplane, N134ZZ, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Vicksburg, Michigan. The airline transport pilot and one passenger were seriously injured. The flight operated under the provisions of Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 as a personal flight. Preliminary information provided by law enforcement indicated the airplane departed from Thrall Lake Airport (7MI3), Vicksburg, Michigan, and climbed to about 1,500 ft when it descended and impacted terrain. Both occupants were airlifted to hospitals, and the airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage and both wings. According to the FAA aircraft records, the airplane was likely a unique build with only the accident airplane currently registered. The airplane was built in 2007 and purchased by the pilot in October 2021. According to a Barnstormers Facebook listing, dated November 8, 2025, the airplane had 210 hours total time, and the engine had 210 hours since major overhaul. Postaccident examination by FAA inspectors revealed the presence of fuel in both fuel tanks. However, when draining fuel from the fuel tanks, an orange substance was found in the fuel line. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260813203582.s: An airline transport pilot and passenger were seriously injured when their experimental Staudacher ZZ 102 impacted terrain near Vicksburg, Michigan, shortly after climbing to 1,500 feet. Postaccident examination found an orange substance in the fuel line, though the specific cause of the descent remains under investigation.

NTSB:20260814203583.n: The pilot reported that during an aerial application flight, the airplane was climbing out from a spray pass along a field when a gust of wind pushed the airplane into a tree, striking the left wing. The pilot was able to maintain control of the airplane and landed without further incident. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the left wing. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260814203583.s: During an aerial application climb, a gust of wind pushed the airplane into a tree, striking the left wing. The pilot maintained control and landed safely, though the aircraft sustained substantial wing damage with no reported mechanical failures.

NTSB:20260816203586.n: On August 15, 2026, 1755 Alaska Daylight Time, a China Airlines Flight Number CI-5265, Boeing 747-400F, registration B-18725, powered by four GE Aerospace CF6-80C2B1F turbofan engines, experienced an inflight fire indication during the initial climb from Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport (PANC). There were no injuries to the 4 crewmembers, and the airplane sustained minor damage. The flight was an international cargo flight from ANC to Taoyuan International Airport (RCTP), Taiwan. According to the pilot, after takeoff at about 5,500ft above mean sea level (MSL), there was an audible fire warning and an "ENG FIRE 3" Engine-Indicating and Crew-Alerting System (EICAS) warning indication illuminated. The crew discharged one fire extinguishing bottle and shutdown the No. 3 engine. During the inflight shutdown procedure, electrical AC Bus Tie 3 tripped and electrical AC Bus 3 de-energized, which resulted in the left-hand autopilot disengaging and the loss of multiple instruments on the captain’s side. The crew engaged the Center autopilot and declared Mayday with air traffic control (ATC). ATC vectored the airplane to a holding pattern to jettison fuel prior to landing, but the fuel jettison control system failed. With the No. 3 engine fire warning no longer illuminated following discharge of the fire extinguishing bottle, the airplane remained in a holding pattern to burn enough fuel to be under the overweight landing limits at PANC. The airplane landed uneventfully approximately two hours after takeoff. A post incident examination of the airplane by maintenance personnel revealed fire damage to a lower section of the left-hand engine cowl and evidence of an undercowl fire on the left-hand side of the engine. The NTSB traveled to the incident site. As part of the investigative process, the NTSB invited qualified parties to participate in the investigation. These included representatives from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), GE Aerospace, and Boeing. The Taiwan Transportation Safety Board (TTSB), representing the State of the Operator, assigned an Accredited Representative; the Civil Aviation Administration (CAA) of Taiwan and China Airlines were named as a technical advisor by the TTSB. The investigation team traveled to ANC to examine the airplane. A pressurization check of the fuel manifolds with nitrogen gas revealed a crack in the left-hand (inboard) fuel manifold tube, located adjacent to fuel nozzle number 24 at approximately the 9 o’clock position on the engine. The engine was later removed from the airplane and shipped to an engine repair and overhaul facility for further examination. This investigation is ongoing..
NTSB:20260816203586.s: China Airlines crew reported an Engine 3 fire warning at 5,500ft during climb, causing electrical failures and autopilot disengagement. A cracked fuel manifold tube caused an undercowl fire, leading to an overweight landing at Anchorage after fuel jettison failed.

NTSB:20260817203588.n: On August 13, 2026, about 1302 central daylight time, a Mooney M20G airplane, N6916N, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Luling, Texas. The pilot received minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 91 personal flight. According to ADS-B data, the flight originated from the David Wayne Hooks Memorial Airport (DWH), Houston, Texas, about 1058. The airplane proceeded to the west-southwest toward San Antonio, Texas, for about an hour. About this time, the pilot contacted San Antonio Approach Control and declared an emergency. The pilot informed the air traffic controller that the airplane's engine had lost power. The controller advised the pilot of an airport 7 miles northeast. The pilot requested a vector to the airport which the controller supplied. The pilot later reported having the airport in-sight before the airplane's position reports ceased. The pilot reported that he executed a forced landing to a road. He said that during the landing roll, the airplane's left wingtip contacted vegetation along the side of the road which pulled the airplane to the left. The main landing gear went onto the shoulder of the road and the airplane veered off the road and struck trees. The airplane sustained substantial damage to its left wing.
NTSB:20260817203588.s: The pilot of a Mooney M20G declared an engine power loss emergency while en route to San Antonio and executed a forced landing on a road. The left wingtip struck vegetation, pulling the aircraft off the road into trees and causing substantial damage to the left wing.

NTSB:20260817203590.n: According to the pilot of the tandem seat biplane, while conducting a short-field landing approach to the runway threshold, he was having trouble seeing his aiming point past the front passenger. He subsequently misjudged the airplane's descent rate during a turn, and the left wing struck a tree beside the runway overrun. The airplane struck the ground and was consumed by a postimpact fire. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260817203590.s: The pilot of a tandem seat biplane misjudged the descent rate during a short-field landing approach after being unable to see the aiming point past the front passenger. The left wing struck a tree, causing the aircraft to crash and burn, with no preaccident mechanical failures reported.

NTSB:20260817203591.n: The pilot reported he was conducting aerial pollination in a corn field. Before beginning the pollination, the pilot flew an inspection circuit around the area to identify potential hazards and observed a center-pivot irrigation system and the power lines along the east and west sides of the field. The pilot reported that he completed about 3/4 of the field pollination and had two passes remaining. While turning the helicopter to enter another pass, the pilot focused on the target row, lost sight of the power lines, and the helicopter struck a power line wire with the tail rotor. Following the wire strike, the pilot elected to perform a precautionary landing. During the landing, the helicopter contacted the ground on the right skid, bounced, and yawed slightly to the right before it came to a stop. A post-accident examination of the helicopter revealed substantial damage to the right rear aft strut mounting area, and damage to the pilot seat floor structure at the forward strut attachment. The pilot reported that there was no evidence of any preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures with the helicopter that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260817203591.s: A helicopter pilot conducting aerial pollination struck a power line with the tail rotor while turning for a pass after losing sight of the hazard. The subsequent precautionary landing resulted in ground contact and structural damage, with no pre-impact mechanical failures identified.

NTSB:20260817203593.n: On August 14, 2026, about 1459 central daylight time, a Gulfstream Aerospace G-IV airplane, N406JS, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near St. Louis, Missouri. The three crew members and 7 passengers were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations part 135 on-demand air taxi flight. According to the crew, they received a STEER BY WIRE FAIL Crew Alerting System (CAS) message before departure from Eagle County Regional Airport (EGE), Eagle, Colorado. They completed the appropriate checklist and the message cleared. While on approach to Runway 8R at Spirit of St. Louis Airport (SUS), St. Louis Missouri, after lowering the landing gear, the crew again received a STEER BY WIRE FAIL CAS message. The crew completed the checklist; however, the message did not clear. The airplane landed on the runway and as the nose wheel contacted the runway it began to shimmy. The nose landing gear (NLG) separated from the airplane followed by a collapse of the left main landing gear. The airplane veered left into the grass and came to rest upright. During the accident sequence, the airplane sustained damage to the lower fuselage and left wing. According to the pilot, during the preflight inspection, the airport ground crew was unable to install the pip pin that goes into the NLG torque link that is used to engage and disengage the scissor link with the Nose Wheel Steering actuator for the NLG. The pilot was able to install the NLG pip pin which has a secondary safety pin that is normally installed into the pip pin to help ensure it remains engaged. The pilot reported that he forgot to install the secondary safety pin. Postaccident examination of the runway and surrounding grass areas found several items of debris. The NLG pip pin, which is normally seated in the NLG torque link, was found separated from the NLG with three ball locks remaining as seen in figure 1. The NLG pip pin normally has four ball locks; the missing ball lock and the NLG upper scissor link could not be located. Examination of the NLG revealed that the safety pin was found intact in the open position and with the separated NLG still attached to its lanyard cord as seen in figure 2. Figure 1. Nose landing gear pip pin. Figure 2. Nose Landing Gear with open safety pin and torque link depicted. The airplane was equipped with a cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder, which were removed and sent to the National Transportation Safety Board Vehicle Recorders Laboratory in Washington, DC, for download. The wreckage was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260817203593.s: The pilot of a Gulfstream G-IV operating a Part 135 flight forgot to install a secondary safety pin on the nose landing gear pip pin during preflight. This omission caused the nose gear to separate upon touchdown at St. Louis, resulting in a collapsed main gear and substantial damage, though all occupants were uninjured.

NTSB:20260817203599.n: The pilot of the tailwheel-equipped airplane reported that while attempting a three-point landing on a grass airstrip, the airplane bounced twice. After the second bounce, the pilot increased engine power and was attempting to abort the landing when he lost control of the airplane. It subsequently nosed over and came to rest inverted on the runway, resulting in substantial damage to the left wing and vertical stabilizer. The pilot did not report that there were any preimpact mechanical malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260817203599.s: The pilot of a tailwheel-equipped airplane lost control while attempting to abort a bounced three-point landing on a grass airstrip. The aircraft nosed over and landed inverted, sustaining substantial damage to the left wing and vertical stabilizer with no reported mechanical malfunctions.

NTSB:20260817203600.n: The pilot reported that during the landing roll on runway 27 he observed three deer crossing the runway. The pilot initiated a go-around and heard a loud bang during the maneuver. The pilot subsequently flew a traffic pattern and returned for landing, unaware that the deer strike had damaged the right main landing gear and separated a portion of the landing gear assembly. During the subsequent landing, the airplane veered to the right and struck a runway marker sign, which resulted in the collapse of the left main landing gear. The airplane then skidded into the grass area adjacent to the runway and came to a stop. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the aft lower fuselage structure. The pilot reported no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airframe or the engine that would have precluded normal operation. A review of the airport directory found a remark to alert pilots to deer on and in the vicinity of the airport.
NTSB:20260817203600.s: The pilot executed a go-around after seeing deer on runway 27, sustaining an undetected right main gear strike. Upon returning to land, the damaged gear caused the aircraft to veer right, strike a sign, collapse the left gear, and skid into grass with substantial fuselage damage.

NTSB:20260817203602.n: On August 14, 2026, about 1945 central daylight time, a Taylorcraft DCO-65 airplane, N48446, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Copper City, Michigan. The pilot was seriously injured. The pilot-rated passenger was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot-rated passenger reported that the takeoff was conducted from a grass airstrip with trees located off the end. The pre-takeoff run-up and magneto check were good, and the engine seemed to be performing normally. However, after becoming airborne, the airplane was not climbing, and the airspeed seemed to be near stall. As the trees became closer, the pilot intentionally turned the airplane to avoid a direct collision. During that turn, the airplane stalled and subsequently impacted the ground. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260817203602.s: The pilot of a Taylorcraft DCO-65, N48446, was seriously injured when the aircraft stalled and impacted the ground near Copper City, Michigan, during takeoff from a grass airstrip. The accident occurred after the pilot turned to avoid trees while the airplane failed to climb and approached stall speed.

NTSB:20260817203603.n: On August 12, 2026, at approximately 2305 eastern daylight time, a Robinson R44 Raven II helicopter, N861MP, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Anthony, Florida. The pilot and passenger sustained minor injuries. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the pilot he had departed a private residence and had climbed to about 700 ft agl when the helicopter started to shake violently. Shortly thereafter the low rotor rpm warning system came on, the pilot lowered the collective and entered an autorotation. During the autorotation, the pilot applied full throttle and the engine and rotor rpm recovered into the normal operating range. As the pilot initiated a climb the engine lost all power again and the pilot made an emergency landing in a field; the helicopter came to rest on its right side. The helicopter is being relocated to a secure location; a detailed examination of the engine and airframe is pending.
NTSB:20260817203603.s: The pilot and passenger of a Robinson R44 Raven II sustained minor injuries when the helicopter was substantially damaged during a Part 91 personal flight near Anthony, Florida. Violent shaking and low rotor rpm warnings led to an autorotation, but the engine lost all power again upon climb initiation, forcing an emergency landing.

NTSB:20260818203608.n: On August 15, 2026, about 1300 eastern daylight time, an experimental, amateur-built Zenith 601 HDS airplane, N601EZ, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Ripley Landing, West Virginia. The private pilot was seriously injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot departed Jackson County Airport, Ravenswood, West Virginia (I18), with the intention of practicing touch and go landings at the airport. The pilot reported that during the left turn onto the downwind leg of the airport traffic pattern, the engine lost all power. The pilot turned the airplane towards the airport but did not have enough altitude to glide to it. The pilot made an emergency off field landing in a tree clearing about 1.2 miles south-southeast of the airport. Upon touchdown, the nose gear impacted terrain, the airplane then nosed over and came to rest inverted. The pilot was trapped under the wreckage until the following day when he was located by first responders about 0900. The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260818203608.s: A private pilot flying an experimental Zenith 601 HDS lost all engine power during a left turn onto the downwind leg while practicing touch-and-go landings. The pilot made an emergency off-field landing in a tree clearing, resulting in substantial damage and serious injury after the aircraft nosed over and came to rest inverted.

NTSB:20260818203609.n: The pilot of the electric motor glider stated that in preparation for decent and landing to the destination airport, he selected the system enable switch to off instead of selecting the motor mast position selector to down. The motor then windmilled, which resulted in the motor and mast losing power, and the glider quickly lost airspeed. The glider then entered an aerodynamic stall and spin. The pilot stated that in an attempt to recover from the spin, he pushed down on the control stick and applied rudder, but the glider pitched up violently. While in an unusual attitude and at a low altitude, the pilot was unable to regain control and deployed the ballistic parachute. During the deployment, the parachute rocket went through the right wing, but the parachute still deployed and the glider impacted terrain in an inverted attitude. The glider sustained substantial damage to the right wing. The pilot attributed the rapid loss of the glider's airspeed due to the drag induced from the windmilling propeller and thought that the windmilling propeller also inhibited airflow over the vertical and horizontal stabilizer, which prevented recovery from the stall and spin. The pilot stated there was no mechanical malfunctions or failures with the glider that precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260818203609.s: The pilot of an electric motor glider selected the system enable switch to off instead of lowering the motor mast during descent, causing the propeller to windmill and induce a stall and spin. Unable to recover at low altitude, the pilot deployed the ballistic parachute, but the glider impacted terrain inverted with substantial right wing damage.

NTSB:20260818203610.n: The flight instructor stated that student pilot was practicing off airport landings in the helicopter. After conducting a normal approach, they transitioned the helicopter into a hover about 2 to 3 ft above the ground. While at a hover, and with both the student pilot and the flight instructor touching the controls, the flight instructor turned his attention to clearing the tail rotor. While the flight instructor's attention was focused outside the helicopter, the helicopter drifted to the left, descended, after which the left skid contacted the ground. The helicopter (dynamically) rolled on to its left side resulting in substantial damage to the fuselage, main rotor system, tail rotor system, and empennage. The flight instructor reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the helicopter that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260818203610.s: During a student helicopter training flight practicing off-airport landings, the aircraft drifted and rolled onto its left side while hovering. The flight instructor attributed the accident to inattention while clearing the tail rotor, noting no mechanical failures occurred.

NTSB:20260818203611.n: On August 14, 2026, about 1040 eastern daylight time, an experimental amateur-built Zenith Cruzer, N673BK, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Chatham, Massachusetts. The pilot and the pilot-rated passenger received minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 flight test. According to the pilot and the owner/builder of the airplane, the accident flight was the airplane's fourth during its phase one testing. The previous three flights were uneventful except for oil temperature anomalies. The owner/builder had adjusted the oil cooler position and the purpose of the accident flight was to verify whether repositioning the oil cooler improved the engine oil temperature readings. The pilot stated that the accident flight was delayed a short time until wind conditions improved. After observing other aircraft operating in the airport traffic pattern, the pilot and the owner/builder decided to proceed with the flight. The preflight inspection, engine runup, and flight control checks were normal. Shortly after takeoff, the pilot reported that the left wing dipped, followed by the right wing, and that the airplane subsequently rocked laterally from side to side. The pilot announced to the owner/builder there was a problem and decided to land the airplane on the remaining runway. Video surveillance footage from the airport showed that the airplane impacted the runway in a left wing down attitude, after which the main landing gear collapsed and the nosewheel separated from the fuselage. The wreckage was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260818203611.s: During a Part 91 flight test of an experimental Zenith Cruzer, the pilot and owner/builder experienced lateral rocking shortly after takeoff while verifying oil cooler adjustments. The aircraft impacted the runway left-wing down, collapsing the main gear and separating the nosewheel, causing minor injuries and substantial damage.

NTSB:20260818203613.n: On August 17, 2026, about 1446 central daylight time, an Aviat Aircraft Inc A-1B airplane, N299CA, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Pilot Grove, Minnesota. The two pilots received minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 aerial photography flight. The pilot in the rear seat stated they were conducting an aerial photography flight and had flown for about 5 ½ hours that day. During the flight, the front seat pilot was manipulating the flight controls and noted that the airplane was not responding normally. They observed that the left aileron had partially detached from the wing and the outboard end was hanging down. The front seat pilot executed an emergency landing to a field. During the landing, the airplane nosed over and sustained substantial damage to both wings and the empennage. Postaccident examination of the airplane revealed that the left outboard aileron hinge bracket was fractured. The airplane was retained for further examination. A review of NTSB records revealed that the airplane was involved in a similar accident in 2017 involving an inflight failure of the left outboard aileron hinge bracket assembly.
NTSB:20260818203613.s: Two pilots flying an Aviat A-1B on an aerial photography mission experienced a partial left aileron detachment due to a fractured hinge bracket. The pilot executed an emergency field landing where the aircraft nosed over, sustaining substantial damage to the wings and empennage.

NTSB:20260819203620.n: The instrument-rated pilot had planned a cross-country flight with an intermediate fuel stop. While enroute, he noted that the weather conditions at the planned fuel stop airport had deteriorated, so he elected to divert to another airport. While performing an RNAV instrument approach to the diversionary airport, the pilot reported that he entered instrument meteorological conditions and experienced "some disorientation." He described that the airplane may have deviated left of course and descended below the glidepath. The pilot subsequently decided to initiate a missed approach and applied full engine power. During the initial climb, the airplane contacted treetops but continued to climb. The pilot observed damage to the left wing and declared an emergency with air traffic control. The air traffic controller then provided the pilot with radar vectors to another airport, where the pilot completed an instrument approach and landed without further incident. A postaccident examination of the airplane revealed that the wings and horizontal stabilizer were substantially damaged. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260819203620.s: An instrument-rated pilot flying an RNAV approach in IMC experienced disorientation, deviated below the glidepath, and struck treetops during a missed approach climb. The pilot declared an emergency, received radar vectors to another airport, and landed safely despite substantial damage to the wings and horizontal stabilizer.

NTSB:20260820203624.n: On August 19, 2026, at 1852 eastern daylight time, a Bell Helicopter Textron Canada 407, N873ST, and a Cessna 150H airplane, N23330, collided in flight near Carlisle, Pennsylvania. The two commercial pilots onboard the helicopter were seriously injured, and the helicopter was substantially damaged. The commercial pilot on board the airplane was fatally injured and the airplane was destroyed. The helicopter was operated by the Pennsylvania State Police (PSP) as a public aircraft. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the PSP, the helicopter crew departed from Capital City Airport (CXY), Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, and flew to Carlisle Airport (N94), Carlisle, Pennsylvania, about 15 nautical miles away, to conduct flight instruction training exercises at the airport. ADS-B flight track data obtained from the FAA revealed the helicopter crew flew a straight in approach to runway 28 at N94 and crossed about 50 ft above the runway threshold at 1851. The helicopter then slowly descended and transitioned into a hover taxi about 1,800 ft down the 4,008-ft-long runway before exiting the paved surface to the north over a grass-covered field. While the helicopter was approaching the airport, ADS-B data showed that the airplane crossed over the airport to the northeast, then made left turns to enter a left crosswind leg to downwind leg of the traffic pattern for runway 28 (figure 1). A witness stated that he heard the airport Common Traffic Advisory Frequency (CTAF) communications between the helicopter flight crew and the airplane pilot; one of the helicopter pilots told the airplane pilot to extend his downwind. The airplane pilot acknowledged the communication. Figure 1 – ADS-B flight track data for the helicopter (green) and airplane (yellow) during their approaches to the airport. During a postaccident interview, the flight instructor onboard the helicopter stated that they saw the airplane on the helicopter’s Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System first, then saw the airplane while it was on the crosswind leg of the airport traffic pattern. The flight instructor then made a radio call stating the helicopter’s position on final approach. The airplane pilot asked if they wanted him to extend his downwind, and the flight instructor responded, “yes, extend your downwind.” The airplane pilot acknowledged and stated that he was number two for landing. Airport surveillance video combined with ADS-B flight track data showed that the pilot turned onto the left base leg of the traffic pattern about 2,500 ft from the runway 28 threshold and continued his approach. Shortly after the pilot initiated the left turn onto base leg, ADS-B track data was lost. Airport surveillance video captured the remainder of the flight. There were three security cameras on the airport that captured the aircraft immediately before and during (figure 2) the approach of both aircraft. Timestamped airport security camera footage showed the helicopter on short final approach to runway 28. The helicopter crossed over the runway threshold while the airplane was on the left base leg. About 30 seconds later, the airplane crossed over the threshold as the helicopter was still over the runway. The airplane’s wings rocked to the left and right as the airplane flew low over the runway surface, and it appeared to make several lateral and vertical movements as it flew over the runway with the flaps extended. The airplane did not touch down on the runway. As the airplane approached the helicopter, the helicopter hovered off the runway and transitioned over the grass field, with its nose still oriented toward the departure end of runway 28 and parallel to the runway. The helicopter pilots stated that due to the helicopter’s position and orientation relative to the runway, they were unable to observe the approaching airplane, which was behind them. Figure 2: Airport security camera locations labeled A, B, and C, showing their orientation relative to the airplane and helicopter’s direction of travel down runway 28. The airplane continued to fly along the runway with the wings rocking before it pitched up and began climbing. After the airplane reached the apex of its climb, about 1 1/2 wingspans above the runway, the right wing dropped and the airplane immediately turned right and descended towards the northwest. The helicopter was in a hover about 50 ft north of the runway when the approaching airplane’s wings rolled level, before it rapidly pitched up, and collided with the rear of the helicopter, striking the tail rotor and main rotor blades. About 8 seconds elapsed from the time the helicopter exited the runway surface until the collision. The following four still video images (figure 3) from two of the airport security cameras show the time, locations, orientation of the aircraft and their relative position to each other. Figure 3 Four still video images from cameras A and C showing the airplane and helicopter as they maneuvered in the vicinity of the runway. The airplane is circled in yellow, and the helicopter is circled in blue. Following the collision, the helicopter’s main rotor blades and tail boom separated. The main wreckage of the helicopter, consisting of the entirety of the fuselage, cockpit, engine, and transmission remained relatively intact and fell onto its left side before coming to rest. During the collision, the airplane separated into four major sections; the engine compartment, wings, empennage, and lower fuselage were spread over a distance of about 250 ft along a magnetic heading of about 330°. Additional parts of the airplane were significantly fragmented and spread throughout the area in a fanlike pattern. All major portions of the helicopter and the airplane were accounted for at the accident site and recovered. Damage signatures to both aircraft including paint transfer marks, and cuts to the fuselages were indicative of a collision. Postaccident examination of both aircraft revealed no evidence of any preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation. During the onsite examination of the airplane, the flaps actuators were observed to be in the retracted position. The wreckage of both aircraft, along with avionics capable of recording digital data were recovered and retained for further examination.
